item.content:encoded:
Promotion: as part of Frieze Seoul 2026, Korean retail giant Shinsegae Group exhibited the meditative work of French artist Paul Cox, which also highlighted the group's focus on weaving art and culture into everyday spaces.

From 2 - 5 September, the exhibition space – named Shinsegae Lounge – featured L'Immensité du Quotidien: The Monumental Everyday, displaying 336 works from Cox's Diary series, which were presented publicly for the first time.

Hung across the walls were hundreds of Cox's gouache paintings, displaying everyday objects and scenes, from buildings and trees to fields and pathways.

According to Shinsegae Group, each painting grew out of Cox's daily meditative practice. Throughout the exhibition, the works are featured chronologically, revealing the evolution of his creative process, from simple line drawings to structured blocks of colour.

Individually, each piece represents a different scene, yet when viewed holistically, they merge together to represent a cohesive landscape.

"Individually modest in scale, together the works accumulate into a monumental landscape shaped by repetition, observation and time," said Shinsegae Group.

As visitors made their way through Frieze Seoul 2026, the exhibition aimed to offer a reflective space, prompting guests to contemplate the beauty of simple, everyday scenes that might otherwise go unseen.

"Against the pace of an international art fair, that attention to the familiar offers a quiet counterpoint, inviting visitors to look longer at what might otherwise pass unseen," the group added.

Shinsegae Group is one of South Korea's leading retail groups, anchored by Emart, the country's largest hypermarket chain, and Shinsegae Department Store, a prominent name in Korean luxury retail.

The company explained that this year's Frieze Seoul 2026 exhibition was designed based on its chairman Chung Yong-jin's belief that "retail should offer more than transactions".

Similarly to the curation of Shinsegae Lounge, Shinsegae Group aims to integrate art and culture into its portfolio of spaces to "give people a reason to linger".

Cox's exhibition marked Shinsegae Group's five-year partnership as the headline partner of Frieze in Seoul.

Throughout the five-year period, Shinsegae Group intends to carry its cultural philosophy throughout the partnership, developing experiences at the intersection of the retail and art sectors, whilst also supporting the global growth and visibility of Korea's art market.

The group also aims to strengthen Seoul as a platform for exchange between Korean and international artists, galleries, collectors and cultural institutions.

"Through innovative projects that redefine the customer experience, Shinsegae Group continues to shape the future of retail and urban lifestyle in Korea," the company explained.

Shinsegae Group has expanded its portfolio and now spans e-commerce, hotels and leisure, food and beverage, fashion, lifestyle, construction, IT, venture investment, and professional sports.

Its commitment to "bringing art into everyday life" began in 1963, with the opening of the Shinsegae Gallery, the first art gallery established by a Korean retailer.

item.content:encoded:
US studio Desai Chia Architecture has referenced the form of "native oak leaves" in shaping the metal roof on Chatham Residence, a rural house in New York designed for retirement.

Located in the town of Chatham in Columbia County, the house sits on the crest of an 80-acre (32-hectare) property near the Catskill Mountains. The area features rolling hills covered in trees and meadows.

The clients — a couple with grown children — desired a home where they could lead "a new life away from New York City".

While designing the project, Manhattan-based Desai Chia Architecture considered all aspects of the landscape, from the distant mountains to the site's relationship to the surrounding forest.

"Much of the understorey was still clear, allowing tree trunks to extend skyward like columns," the team said.

"The shadows cast by the leafy canopy revealed arcs of light and shadow that playfully shifted with the sunlight."

For the bucolic site, the studio created a single-level home topped with a sculptural roof with deep overhangs.

"The roof was inspired by native oak leaves," the team said.

"Curved overhangs provide shade and protection from the elements while also casting shadows that mimic nature."

Exterior walls are clad in corrugated metal siding, which is meant to appear "as a continuous ripple that traces the curved shapes".

"We decided on corrugated metal for its duality – a rugged material frequently used in contemporary farm buildings, as well as an elegant surface that captures light with minimalist precision," the team said.

The exterior also features plain-sawn accoya wood, which was used for soffits and covered seating areas.

The central portion of the house contains the social zone, with a kitchen, dining area and living room. Curved corners soften the transition between walls and a vaulted ceiling, helping form "a cloud of luminosity".

Floor-to-ceiling glass provides views of the scenic terrain.

Read:

Desai Chia uses "camouflaging effect" for secluded Osprey House in New York

"The clients enjoy views from the forest understorey to the tree canopy to the sky," the studio said.

The central zone is flanked by two wings – one contains the primary bedroom, the other holds additional bedrooms.

Beyond large stretches of glass, daylight sneaks in through "hidden" clerestory windows in the primary bathroom and entry hall.

In addition to the main residence, the project included a detached guesthouse, which also holds the couple's home office.

This "sister building" takes cues from the main residence, as it features corrugated metal siding and curved overhangs. Large sliding doors allow the interior to flow onto a pool terrace.

The team also created a greenhouse and barn, designed by Desai Chia in collaboration with New Hampshire-based Rimol Greenhouses.

With polycarbonate walls, the structures absorb sunlight during the day and "glow like lanterns at night".

In terms of the landscape, the team planned grazing pastures for sheep, goats, miniature donkeys and other animals, which frame a pathway to a natural pond.

The project was designed as a second home, but the clients envision living there full-time in the future. They've already begun raising animals on the site and growing plants in the greenhouse.

"What began as an escape from the city has become the start of a second act," the team said.

Other projects by Desai Chia include a house on a secluded New York island clad in charred wood and a multi-structure dwelling in Connecticut that has courtyards for exhibiting artwork.

item.content:encoded:
Local designer Rafael Prieto has created a collection of furniture using cast-offs of a Tribeca facade for his latest exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery in New York City.

For The Future of the Past exhibition, Prieto used sixteen salvaged pieces from the renovation of an early twentieth-century building that was taking place across from his New York studio.

According to the team, Prieto "became deeply interested" in the ornamental pieces from the building during the renovation project, and eventually arranged to have them preserved.

He held them in his studio for a year before working with them, mulling over their "history, meaning, and potential" and their connection to the city at large.

"For Prieto, the fragments became a way of thinking about New York itself", said the team.

The collection includes four tables that incorporate the actual architectural pieces, including a chunk of a cornice, while other objects, such as a bright red chair, contain lines and motifs that were abstracted from the discarded building bits.

Prieto built out around the architectural stone with contemporary colours and materials, such as lacquered birch wood painted in deep purple, black and red, or an exposed-burl veneer.

The Red Birch and Stone Table, for instance, stands on one leg made of an architectural corbel, one leg made of bright red striated birch, and a top of birch with burl veneer.

Read:

Tian & Teague creates home decor informed by the "discomforts" of New York

Other pieces in the collection include a stool with a fragment wedged in the centre and a low-lying burl veneer chair with red geometric arm supports.

"The dichotomy between these materials – the hard and the soft, the historic and the contemporary – runs throughout the collection," said the team.

Displayed at Emma Scully Gallery, the collection is surrounded by a wallpaper designed by Prieto and Wallpaper Projects, which depicts Prieto's photography.

Prieto, who is originally from Mexico, also runs marketing studio Savvy between New York and Mexico City. He also founded a chocolate company.

Local designers often take inspiration from New York City, interpreting their personal experiences through made objects. Recent work includes a chair by Italian designer Massimiliano Malagò that is a reflection on why he continually returns to the city and delicate lamps designed by Bechara Maalouf made with wood scraps from old building beams.

The photography is by Clement Pascal.

The Future of the Past is on view at Emma Scully Gallery in the Upper East Side from 30 September to 12 December. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Florida-based Nothing has created hot and cold paper takeaway cups with built-in lids that are designed to be compostable.

In the past two years, Nothing has created two versions of its proprietary cups, which feature elongated sides that fold down to become lids and a water-based coating that allows for at-home composting.

It hopes that these designs will propel it to becoming a household name in the paper cup market.

"If you were to stop anyone on the street, they could maybe name one or two cup companies, maybe just one," Nothing co-founder Brandon Leeds told Dezeen. "The goal is to be the other one."

First manufacturing paper straws, co-founders Brandon and Jordan Leeds, a coder and a product designer, respectively, became disillusioned by what they saw as greenwashing in the field, with companies serving paper straws in plastic cups.

"We thought it was weird that paper straws were being put into plastic cups with plastic lids, and that's when we had the idea for a cup with a built-in lid," Brandon Leeds said.

Created at a time when researchers have shown that some bioplastics do not degrade at the rate originally thought, the goal was to create a product that was usable while being "sustainable".

The cups are designed to decompose in 180 days and are accredited for home composting with TÜV's OK compost HOME – a certification that verifies a product will decompose in a low-heat, back garden environment.

They are coated with a water-based coating that binds to the paper fibres when they are being formed. Called aqueous dispersion, this method often still features plastic elements, but Brandon Leeds said that the coating they used does not and is certified plastic-free by European product certification body Flustix.

"The cup is then recyclable and also home compostable," he said.

The body of the cup itself is slightly triangular and was designed to fit into the hand. The hot cup has three flaps that fold together and lock down, with a spout for drinking, while the cold cup has four folds that come together and an insert for a straw.

"It's more spill-resistant than a traditional cup and lid," said Brandon Leeds.

As the Nothing cups don't have separate lids, packaging and shipping costs are reduced as well as material costs. According to Brandon Leeds, this also solves storage problems for businesses, as cup lids in bulk take up space in a restaurant.

Read:

Heliograf launches plastic-free alternative to single-use soy sauce fish

Although the company is working with thousands of vendors in the US and Canada, Brandon Leeds said he expects some people to be resistant to the change.

"The paper cup was invented in 1907, and nothing has changed in all this time until our cup, so it's been a long time," he said. "People like what they like, and when there's change, they are not always the most open to it, until it becomes the norm."

"You heard so much about paper straws in 2018, 2019," he continued. Now no one even talks about them."

The material content of our drinking materials has become an issue beyond the design world, with Donald Trump taking a stance against paper straws in a 2025 executive order phasing out government use of plastic straw alternatives.

Others have insisted on reusable cups as the best solution to waste produced by to-go containers. Last year, Seymourpowell combined a resueable water bottle and coffee thermos into a single product.

The photography is courtesy of Nothing.

item.content:encoded:
Stepping stones lead across a reflective pool of water at Lech Mountain Mirror, a viewpoint in the Austrian Alps, designed by architecture studio Snøhetta to invite a moment of pause.

Located in a village called Lech in the Vorarlberg region, the installation comprises a shallow pool of water on the roof of the Zugerbergbahn cable car station, across which visitors can walk.

Snøhetta's Innsbruck office designed Lech Mountain Mirror as a lookout point that simultaneously mirrors the dramatic views of the surrounding mountains and clouds, playing with visitors' perspectives.

Free to access, it is hoped to become a popular tourist attraction that could help position Lech as a year-round destination, rather than just for winter skiing.

"The Lech Mountain Mirror transforms an infrastructure facility into a place for sensory experience," said Snøhetta partner Patrick Lüth.

"It captures the magic of the mountains for visitors in an unusual way and offers opportunities to admire the mountain world from a different perspective."

Lech Mountain Mirror comprises a series of striped stepping stones in the pool of water, which lead up to a rock rising from its surface.

Within the water, visitors can see a mirror image of the surrounding landscape that shifts with the weather and time of day, inviting visitors to pause and observe the ever-changing landscape.

"The weather becomes part of the experience, constantly altering one's perception of the surroundings," said Snøhetta.

"On sunny, clear days, you see a precise reflection."

Read:

Snøhetta cantilevers viewpoint from mountain overlooking Innsbruck

"When the wind blows, the reflection blurs, and the ripples on the water's surface create a new natural experience," the studio continued.

"The reflections of mountains and sky, clouds and people merge into an image that changes with every breath of wind and every shift in light."

Surrounding the lookout is a green space and various seating areas made from larch wood and stone boulders.

Snøhetta said the installation is among several art initiatives under development in the area to boost summer tourism, including projects by artists Antony Gormley and James Turrell.

Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. Nearby in the Nordkette mountain range, the Innsbruck office also created the Path of Perspectives – a series of architectural interventions for a mountain walking trail.

Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include a double-helix structure for bird watching in China and a converted antenna tower in the Swiss Alps by Herzog & de Meuron.

The photography is by Christian Flatscher.

item.content:encoded:
A distinctive roof maximises mountain views and prevents snow build-up at this timber-framed house in Japan's Shimane Prefecture, designed by Japanese studio Enter-Archi.

Named House in Yakami after the rural town where it is located, the one-storey home was organised by Enter-Archi as three connected volumes with courtyards in between.

A covered parking space occupies the front volume, while the middle one contains an open-plan living, kitchen and dining room, and the rear volume hosts three bedrooms.

The house was constructed from a traditional Japanese timber post-and-beam system, with columns, beams and rafters left exposed.

A broken-pitch roof spans House in Yakami's three sections.

The gentler angle of the upper pitch helps keep the roof height low, maintaining views of the surrounding mountains, while the steeper lower pitch echoes the tiled roofs of the neighbouring buildings and helps prevent snow from piling up.

"By reducing the upper portion to a two-in-ten pitch and keeping the overall height low, views from the interior are drawn beyond the building towards the sky and mountains," Enter-Archi founder Yoshikatsu Iriguchi told Dezeen.

"In the living, dining and kitchen space, the ceiling height was also carefully adjusted to create a sense of bodily scale while maintaining the openness of the space."

Read:

Keiji Ashizawa clads House in Yatsugatake in charred cedar

The open layout of the central living space and its adjacent courtyards was designed to give the residents space to relax with family and friends.

Iriguchi also wanted the low-lying house to nestle into the rural landscape.

"Fields and mountain ranges extend to the east and west, while houses with traditional Sekishu-tile roofs line the north and south," said Iriguchi. "Mist settles over the area in the mornings and evenings, and in winter the landscape is covered in snow, creating a landscape distinctive to this place."

"Within this setting, there were two main themes," he continued. "The first was not to simply consume the beautiful landscape as a view, but to place oneself within it and engage with it through bodily perception."

"The second was to accept that architecture, too, can be gradually eroded by the landscape, while seeking a distinct order that remains intact and exploring the universal possibilities of architecture."

Everyday materials were chosen to finish the building, including metal roofing, cedar cladding on the exterior and plywood walls in the interior.

"Familiar materials and finishes commonly found in Japanese timber architecture were used with the intention of creating the architecture from materials that are as simple and unpretentious as possible," said Iriguchi.

Elsewhere in Japan, Keiji Ashizawa Design recently created an angular home clad in cedar, while YNAS has updated a traditional timber house by adding timber-framed canopies.

The photography is by Yoshikatsu Iriguchi.

item.content:encoded:
Experimental clothing brand Vollebak has made a one-off coat covered in over 50,000 half-centimetre-square pieces of slate.

Named Rock Jacket, the coat is the latest piece designed by Vollebak that aims to challenge traditional clothing material choices. It follows jackets made from graphene, copper, American walnut and Dyneema – a fibre that is 15 times stronger than steel.

"We have made clothing with wood, mycelium, and metal, rock felt like one of the next logical challenges to take on," Vollebak co-founder Nick Tidball told Dezeen.

Described by the brand as a "sci-fi-style Harrington jacket", the coat is entirely covered in five millimetre by five millimetre slate tiles.

In total, there are around 54,000 of these micro tiles on the jacket that are each half a millimetre thick and were attached to a neoprene base layer.

According to Tidball, slate is the most ambitious material the brand has made a jacket from, and the abundance of rock in the world means that it should be seriously considered as a material for clothing.

"At Vollebak we are aiming to create technological and material breakthroughs in clothing. Rock definitely represents a potential new material frontier," said Tidball.

"The first [reason to do this] would be, once you make a jacket out of rock everything else seems easy," he continued. "And the second would be, seeing as it's one of the most abundant materials on the planet, we should start looking to see if it's a viable material for clothing."

Made in collaboration with French material technologist Steven Leprizé, the Rock Jacket builds on processes developed for the brand's Wooden Jacket, which was made from 250,000 pieces of laser-cut American walnut.

The elastic marquetry technique, known as WooWood, that was used for the wooden jacket was adapted for slate with the latest creation.

Read:

Vollebak creates prototype Wooden Jacket from 250,000 pieces of American walnut

Leprizé highlighted the precise laser cutting of the tiles into exact squares that allow the jacket to bend as the most important part of the jacket's production.

"There are 50 steps to making this material," said Leprizé, "and the cutting of the tiles is the most important."

According to the brand, the jacket aims to challenge the idea of throw-away clothing by utilising a material that "took millions of years to form" and also to "rethink our relationship with the oldest materials".

Vollebak now aims to develop the idea to create a commercially viable jacket that it hopes to release in two years.

"No one has really attempted to make a jacket from stone before, you experience serious creative and fabrication challenges at every turn," added Tidball.

"From sourcing the material, to constructing the material, to bonding the material, to constructing the jacket, there have been so many moments between the conception and the near completion of the Rock Jacket that looked like this project could have ended."

In architecture, stone is also being reconsidered as a modern material, with a high-rise block in London recently completed with a structural stone exoskeleton.

The photography is courtesy of Vollebak.

Dezeen Showroom: acoustic solutions brand Zilenzio has released Zonify Wall and Zonify Table, a duo of sound-absorbing products for streamlining in-person and digital meetings.

Created in collaboration with Studio Stockholm, Zonify Wall is a large, wall-mounted acoustic panel, while Zonify Table is a smaller desk screen with integrated dimmable lighting.

Both products feature a distinctive pleated textile design made up of stone wool and fabric, selected for maximum sound absorption in an office environment.

Studio Stockholm founder Marco Checchi had the idea for the pleated design during a dinner, when he folded a napkin and began to envision the acoustic solutions that the brand described as quick and easy to install.

Designed for a range of office or commercial environments, Zonify Wall comes in roll form and is available in several heights and fabrics. Users can also attach stone wool behind the fabric to enhance sound absorption.

Zonify Table was created with hybrid work in mind, which has seen an increase in digital meetings. The table attaches directly to a desktop and can be plugged into a standard wall outlet.

"Hybrid work has raised expectations for digital meetings, yet many focus rooms still lack good acoustics and lighting," said Zilenzio. "Zonify Table brings both into one product."

item.content:encoded:
A passage for migratory fish and a cycle route have been added to Afsluitdijk, an iconic dam in the Netherlands, in a recent revamp by Dutch studio Benthem Crouwel.

Afsluitdijk is a landmark 32-kilometre-long dam built between 1927 and 1932 to protect the Netherlands from storm surges and flooding caused by the North Sea.

It was updated over the last eight years to align with current safety standards and improve its performance against increasingly extreme weather and rising sea levels.

According to Benthem Crouwel, the overhaul ensures the dam can withstand a severe one-in-10,000-year storm, while preserving its iconic character and long, linear form.

"The Afsluitdijk is one of the Netherlands' most iconic waterworks and a landmark of Dutch water engineering," studio partner Daniel Jongtien told Dezeen.

"The significance of the Afsluitdijk is huge on many levels. It was built in the 1930s to close off the former Zuiderzee, creating the IJsselmeer and fundamentally changing how the country manages water," Jongtien explained.

"The brief was to strengthen the iconic and monumental character of the Afsluitdijk without losing sight of its primary function."

With a quarter of the country below sea level, marine engineering infrastructure is a common sight throughout the Netherlands. Afsluitdijk is one of the most notable examples, separating the IJsselmeer lake from the Wadden Sea.

Benthem Crouwel has been developing its revamp since 2018 with construction company BAM and contractor Van Oord, alongside investors Rebel and Invesis. This group will continue to maintain and oversee the project for 25 years.

As part of the project, the studio reinforced the entire length of the structure with 75,000 interlocking concrete blocks called Levvel-blocs and raised it by two metres.

The blocks are arranged in a deliberately symmetrical and regular pattern, and finished with rough surfaces onto which marine vegetation can latch.

Read:

Schønherr combines flood defence with urban park in Copenhagen

The team has also introduced additional pumping stations and discharge sluices – water channels that regulate flow – as well as storm surge barriers, a fish passage and a cycle path.

Benthem Crouwel said its overarching goal was simplicity and ensuring any visible elements "reveal how the infrastructure works and enhances the experience of the Afsluitdijk".

"The design is characterised by spectacular simplicity – abstract in form and minimalist in detail," said Jongtien.

"The architecture is restrained, allowing the function of the dike to remain visible while supporting technology is kept out of sight," he continued. "At the same time, where elements are made visible, they have a clear functional and architectural purpose."

Among the most notable additions is the series of six pumping stations, housed in four-metre-high domes. These are "one of the few deliberately visible architectural elements added to the Afsluitdijk", Benthem Crouwel said.

These pumps discharge excess water from the IJsselmeer into the Wadden Sea.

"The almost 12-metre-high pumps beneath them discharge 275,000 litres of water per second, comparable to filling an Olympic swimming pool in nine seconds," said the studio.

Meanwhile, a 15-metre-wide opening carved into the structure provides a new passage for fish to move between the IJsselmeer and the Wadden Sea – reinstating an important migratory zone between salt and fresh water that the structure blocked for almost a century.

"It represents a shift in thinking: from simply keeping water out to balancing flood protection with ecological connectivity," Jongtien explained.

Completing the project is a cycle and pedestrian route, positioned on the side of the Wadden Sea.

It incorporates viewpoint platforms and aims to give users "a more direct experience of the scale of the Afsluitdijk". An existing route on the IJsselmeer side was retained.

Other major infrastructure projects recently featured on Dezeen include Denmark's 300,000-square-metre land reclamation project and the Sydney Harbour Bridge Cycleway Ramp.

Promotion: Spanish design brand Kriskadecor has clad the facade of Disneyland Paris's latest store in a striking aluminium chain system that reinterprets the visuals of "it's a small world" – one of the resort's most popular attractions.
Disney Glamour, Disney Village's latest shop within the "it's a small world" universe, was designed to have an "instantly recognisable and timeless" aesthetic.

The building's facade features a lightweight epoxy-coated aluminium chain facade developed by Kriskadecor, known as a KDO Fixed System.

The design aimed to reinterpret Disney artist Mary Blair's "it's a small world" graphic, whose whimsy and colourful style has defined Disney's musical attraction since its launch in the 1970s.

Measuring 14.66 metres wide and 5.8 metres high, the chains create a lightweight, visually striking volume, which gives the building a strong architectural presence.

Using Blair's signature palette of blue, gold and white, the design also mirrors her geometrical compositions and graphic architectural motifs.

"At Disney Glamour, Kriskadecor's aluminium chains recreate a pattern inspired by Blair's collage-like approach, evoking temples, minarets and international silhouettes reminiscent of the celebrated facade of "it's a small world", said the brand about its system.

"The composition employs five colours, carefully selected to honour Blair's artistic language: bright whites, deep blues and warm golds."

According to Kriskadecor, the facade interacts with changing light patterns throughout the day, giving the building an ever-changing appearance.

"Located in an area accessible year-round, the new store has quickly become a visual landmark within the retail and leisure district, reinforcing the character of its surroundings and enriching the visitor experience with an instantly recognisable and timeless aesthetic," said Kriskadecor.

Externally, the facade is a continuous, solid-looking surface that provides privacy. Internally, the chain ensures visibility, whilst promoting natural ventilation.

The system is also designed to reduce solar heat gain and improve the building's overall thermal comfort in hot weather conditions.

According to Kriskadecor, the use of aluminium ensures the chains are corrosion-resistant and fully recyclable, aligning with "contemporary sustainability principles in architecture and construction".

The system was also tested to withstand variable wind pressures, and its flexible design ensures installation and maintenance are straightforward.

Like the Disney store's facade, Kriskadecor's facade solutions are customisable in size, form and colour, allowing the reproduction of images, patterns and logotypes.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: Danish eyewear brand Lindberg has presented a site-specific installation for the Armory Show in New York City, created with Italian artist Fabrizio Corneli.

Called Enigma of Vision, the minimalist installation opened on 24 September as part of the city's annual Armory Show of contemporary art. From 10 to 15 November, the installation will also feature at the West Bund Art and Design in Shanghai.

Lindberg, which distinguishes itself from other eyewear brands through its sharp, architectural approach to design, commissioned Corneli to design the site-specific work for the exhibition.

Enigma of Vision presents two interconnected artworks by Corneli, whose portfolio of site-specific pieces is defined by experiments with light and shadow.

The first is Seed, a sculpture featuring a concealed light source. When visitors interact with the sculpture, it reveals an image of the globe.

Lindberg explained that the piece encourages visitors to reflect on humanity's connected future through the interplay of space, form and light.

The second artwork is called Eyecatcher. This piece centres on a selection of Lindberg's most recognisable glasses, transforming the frames into sources of striking shadows, which are a familiar motif in Corneli's work.

Together, both pieces express Lindberg's philosophy of stripping away design to its essential parts, while also exploring how perception is shaped equally by what we see and "what remains hidden".

Since 1986, Lindberg has been producing lightweight glasses in materials like titanium gold, platinum, buffalo horn, fine wood and diamonds, without the need for screws or rivets.

The brand has since ventured into the art world and has been an active participant in the industry since 1986.

Lindberg was first present at the Armory Show in 2024, when it collaborated with American photography and sculpture artist Letha Wilson.

Last year, Brooklyn-based artist Yuko Nishikawa created a Lindberg installation of delicate sculptural mobiles for the show.

The brand considers Enigma of Vision to be a progression of Lindberg's commitment to the arts.

"Lindberg's collaboration with Corneli is a natural extension of the brand's design philosophy, where technical mastery and artistic expression converge to challenge perception and reveal beauty through simplicity," said the founder, president, and CEO of Kering Eyewear, which owns Lindberg, Roberto Vedovotto.

To learn more about Lindberg, visit its website here.

Enigma of Vision takes place from 10 to 15 November at the West Bund Art and Design in Shanghai. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Mexican architecture studio Chain + Siman has created a weekend house with a series of contemporary gables that connects to a stone-clad bunkhouse in Valle de Bravo, outside of Mexico City.

Known as Casa Ani, the 689-square-metre residence was completed in 2025, a few hours from the Chain + Siman studio in Mexico City.

The studio's design was informed by a gabled structure that had long stood on the property.

The team drew this heritage form into a single-roofed, stone-and-timber house and a contemporary three-gabled structure wrapped in black standing-seam metal.

"Casa Ani grew out of a dialogue between old and new," Chain + Siman told Dezeen.

"The result is a conversation across materials and time: stone against metal, tile against steel, the weight of history against the lightness of the new."

The primary entrance passes through the largest of the three glass gables.

On the east side, the three-gabled form holds the social areas of the house with the living and dining room, kitchen and primary suite encapsulated beneath independent A-frame roofs elevated above floor-to-ceiling glazing.

"Dark metal cladding frames inclined wooden planes, creating a lightweight and rhythmic facade," the studio said.

"The repetition of the A-frame roofs brings dynamism to the composition, while the glazing of the final volume extends across almost its entire elevation, revealing the social areas and reinforcing their open character."

Read:

Estudio Zero shapes pink Mexican co-living complex after sound wave

The largest of these gabled forms holds the living room, centred on a black-steel fireplace set against a palette of warm-toned engineered wood. It looks out onto outdoor seating and a pool.

Set perpendicularly to the contemporary form, the two-story stone building juts along the eastern longitudinal axis of the irregular site.

"This stone structure accommodates the bedrooms and presents a largely closed facade toward the street," the studio said.

"A large window interrupts its solidity, framing a double-height space and a steel staircase that emphasises the contrast between mass and transparency."

A warm-toned family room with a built-in lounging platform is the heart of the stone building, transitioning to a secondary suite and service and storage spaces. Above, three suites extend the sleeping quarters with double porches that traverse the long side of the form.

Surrounded by a landscape designed by Pedro Sánchez Paisajismo, the extensive program extends outdoors into a space in which olive trees, flowering species and an orchard blend into the forest.

"The residence incorporates an off-grid strategy through solar panels and battery storage located on the south-facing metal roofs," the studio said.

"Their formal integration allows them to blend with the architecture, reducing both visual and environmental impact while reinforcing the project’s energy autonomy."

A popular holiday destination on the banks of Lake Avándaro, Valle de Bravo is home to several other recent geometric designs.

Sordo Madaleno divided a house across six red, rounded pavilions, Fernanda Canales oriented a circular house like a solar clock and Pedro & Juana connected an extension with a zigzag tunnel staircase.

The photography is by Rafael Gamo.

item.content:encoded:
A structure made of bio-based thermoplastic and recycled broom heads is among the works featured in a mid-career retrospective of design studio Rael San Fratello at San Francisco's Yerba Buena Center for the Arts.

The exhibition, Rael San Fratello: Prototypes and Provocations, features a range of work by the Oakland-based studio, which was founded in 2002 by designers Virginia San Fratello and Ronald Rael.

Staged at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in downtown San Francisco, the show includes structures, objects, models, film and other elements. It is billed as "the most comprehensive presentation" of the studio's work to date.

Rael San Fratello is known for its material exploration, experimental uses of 3D printing, and engagement with social and political issues.

"Rael San Fratello's work attests to the power of radical imagination grounded in humanistic values and an ethos of play and constant experimentation," said show curator René Morales.

"Blurring the boundaries between architecture and social practice, tradition and technology, poetics and activism, the studio envisions a better world at the same time that it seeks to develop the tools with which we may one day be able to construct for ourselves."

A centrepiece of the show is Sanctuary – a cylindrical structure 3D-printed on-site using a mixture of soil, straw and water. Visitors can walk around and enter the structure, which is topped with a mirrored inflatable orb.

"Sanctuary is made from humankind's oldest building material, constructed using emerging robotic technologies," said the studio.

The earthen walls of the structure are pierced with glass solar rods salvaged from Solyndra, a once-promising local manufacturer of solar panels that filed for bankruptcy in 2011.

"Raw earth has sheltered people for 10,000 years, and the Solyndra rods embedded in its walls point to the complexity of combining contemporary and traditional materials," the studio said.

"Bringing them together creates a space to contemplate what endures, what gets discarded, and what deserves a second chance."

The show also includes a structure called The Workshop, which was commissioned by the arts centre.

It has a roof covered in broom heads that were sourced from an exhibition in Seoul, and undulating facades wrapped in biodegradeable thermoplastic – PLA filament – and small planter boxes.

Read:

Harvard University transforms waste wool into cladding for retrofits

The installation reflects the studio's broader interest in combining locally available and discarded materials with digital fabrication technologies.

A series of display tables show 3D-printed objects made from basic materials such as coffee grounds, Chardonnay grape skins and ash collected in the aftermath of the California wildfires.

Elsewhere, Teeter-Totter Wall, one of the studio's most recognised works, was placed on a white pedestal in front of a wall showing its deployment.

It consists of bright-pink seesaws that in 2019 were extended through openings in the US and Mexico border wall. People on opposite sides were able to interact while riding the seesaws.

"The work invited a playful, transnational exchange and garnered widespread attention as a powerful symbol of the possibility for connection across a deeply contested divide," said the Yerba Buena arts centre.

There are Tyvek coats that can be inflated to serve as temporary shelter, and REUNITE, a poster showing the silhouettes of two parents and a child running toward each other.

The latter project was created as an open-source, downloadable image that could be used in protests.

"Collectively, the works on view speak to Rael San Fratello's ongoing work to develop creative solutions to some of our most challenging social and political issues, while also pioneering ways to incorporate sustainable and often-times unexpected materials into their work," the museum said.

The firm's work includes a series of 3D-printed structures called Mud Frontiers, and a shed clad in hexagon-shaped tiles with openings for growing little succulents.

The photography is by Matthew Millman.

Rael San Fratello: Prototypes and Provocations is on view from  25 September to 31 January 2027. For more exhibitions in architecture and design visit Dezeen Events Guide.

Dezeen Showroom: architecture studio Gensler worked with Danish manufacturer Ege Carpets to produce Our Planet, a collection of landscape-inspired carpets and rugs.

The global architecture and design firm served as product design consultants on Our Planet, exploring how flooring can shape spatial experience and how the underlying structures of nature can serve as inspiration.

The completed collection traces an abstract journey across the American landscape, from the west coast's mountain ranges through to the east's waterways and cultivated terrain.

"Our Planet was inspired by the different ways we perceive the landscape," said Gensler design director Emma Chang. "Up close, it's about texture and topography. From above, it becomes a network of movement and flow."

"Bringing these perspectives together allowed us to create a collection that expresses both the physical and emotional depth of the natural world."

The Our Planet collection is available in multiple formats, including wall-to-wall carpet, planks and rugs, to suit the needs of diverse commercial environments.

The carpets are made in Denmark from wool and recycled polyamide and can be manufactured with a choice of backing systems.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studios Carmody Groarke, Atama and Re-st have completed the revamp of Design Museum Gent in Belgium, adding a geometric volume wrapped in waste-based white bricks.

Set to reopen to the public in Ghent this weekend, the timber-framed wing introduces educational and event spaces to the museum, along with additional exhibition space.

The team, which includes London-based Carmody Groarke and local studios Atama and Re-st, has also restored the museum's three historic wings and renovated an existing courtyard.

Described by the team as the "final piece of the museum site", the extension was designed to unite the museum's collection of previously disjointed spaces, "completing the visitor loop".

It slots behind a portion of the museum's historic facade and, alongside one of the old wings, frames the existing courtyard updated by the studios.

The 2,200-square-metre expansion makes the building Belgium's largest design museum, spanning a total of 8,600 square metres including 3,700 square metres of exhibition space.

"Organisationally, we've got this idea of an ensemble of four buildings," Carmody Groarke co-founder Kevin Carmody told Dezeen during a tour of the building today.

"The new building makes sense of three older buildings by connecting them physically in terms of accessibility, but also making the ensemble orient itself around this beautiful courtyard."

For the extension's design, the studios nodded to Ghent's traditional gabled houses, resulting in its sloping profile and use of limestone bricks.

These bricks, which borrow their dimensions from the neighbouring Hotel de Coninck, were produced using local construction waste before undergoing a low-energy lime-curing process.

Designed with circular economy specialist Local Works Studio and materials manufacturer BC Materials, they are claimed to carry just one-third of the embodied carbon of a typical Belgian clay brick.

Externally, this brick facade is punctuated by a series of boxy glazed openings, including at ground level where a large entrance features a 3D-printed aluminium door created by Antwerp studio Unfold.

Read:

Municipal waste used to form low-carbon brick for Design Museum Gent extension

The six-storey extension opens up to a reception and shop at ground level, where steps framed by an oversized earth column made using on-site construction waste lead up to the courtyard.

The building's programme has been divided into distinct zones, rising from ground-floor exhibition spaces and a lecture hall to education spaces across its middle floors.

An event space crowns the building, complete with expansive windows overlooking the city. Meanwhile, an art-handling area is at basement level.

"[The rooms] respond to the very unusual proportions of the site and connect views specifically to each of the functions," Carmody said. "Each floor is unique in their experience."

Throughout the extension, the wing's timber structure has been left exposed and paired with white walls and wooden floors.

Visitors can also see bio-based design details by various Belgium-based creatives, including furniture by Casimir and Bram Vanderbeke & Wendy Andreu, and a pocket garden by Bureau Bas Smets.

The revitalisation of the museum's historic wings involved the division of its large exhibition space into a series of smaller areas. The museum will reopen to the public on 3 October with a new art collection and opening exhibition.

Other recently completed museums featured on Dezeen include the Mind Museum in Denmark, held within a former psychiatric hospital, and a trio of "wonderfully expressive" buildings designed by Peter Zumthor for the Foundation Beyeler museum in Switzerland.

item.content:encoded:
Danish studio CF Møller has completed the Mind Museum on the island of Funen in Denmark, guided by the "clear spatial structure" of the former psychiatric hospital it occupies.

Located in the town of Middelfart, the Mind Museum tells the history of psychiatry in Denmark and the early 19th-century hospital itself.

CF Møller's ambition was to preserve the bulk of the building, which dates back to 1888, "allowing the existing architecture to remain a central part of the museum".

This involved retaining and restoring the exterior while improving circulation and functionality and adapting the building to meet modern-day regulations.

"The brief was to transform one of the original patient buildings from 1888 at the former psychiatric hospital in Middelfart into Mind Museum while retaining as much as possible of the building's original character and clear spatial structure," studio partner Rune Bjerno Nielsen told Dezeen.

"The institution remained in operation until 1999, so the building is not simply a historic setting for the museum, it is part of the history the museum is interpreting," he continued.

"That gives the museum an authenticity that would have been impossible to recreate elsewhere. Visitors are encountering psychiatric history in the place where that history actually unfolded."

The original building was part of a wider hospital complex originally designed as "a small town" with ample access to daylight and greenery, according to CF Møller.

It is one of six buildings of its kind that remain in Denmark, though only one is still used as a psychiatric hospital.

Inside, Mind Museum contains exhibition areas, public facilities such as a cafe, and meeting and activity spaces. Architectural designer Kumulus Agency oversaw the exhibition areas.

The museum is not only used for learning, but also as a meeting place for people and organisations dedicated to mental health and wellbeing.

"Mind Museum is not intended only as somewhere you consume information; it is a place where people can meet, talk, pause and reflect," said Nielsen. "That helps create a more open setting for subjects that can otherwise be difficult to approach."

According to CF Møller, the organisation of Mind Museum deliberately builds on the existing structure rather than reconfiguring it.

Visitors enter through the reinstated original main entrance, with stairs to the exhibition areas and ticket zone. For Nielsen, this is the highlight of the project.

"The reinstated historic entrance brings visitors back into the building through its original point of arrival," he reflected.

"It condenses the whole transformation into a relatively small part of the building: the historic architecture remains clearly present, but a few contemporary interventions completely change how you understand and move through it."

The ground floor is designed to have "the strongest connection to the original hospital", with a material and colour palette that draws on its original design. Here, the exhibition spaces tell the story of the original building.

Above, the first floor has a deliberately contrasting character, with lighter and more contemporary finishes. Exhibits explore present-day issues and questions around psychiatry and mental wellbeing.

Here, exhibition areas are dotted between former patient rooms, through which new openings have been created to give physical and visual links.

Read:

CF Møller Architects uses principles of "healing architecture" for Finnish psychiatric clinic

"The historic layer stays on the ground floor, where visitors step into history, and the upper floor is designed for variation and contemporary storytelling," explained Nielsen.

"Visitors move between spaces with different atmospheres and intensities, rather than through one continuous exhibition environment."

Completing the project is a basement that now functions as a series of spaces for group activities hosted by specialist associations and community groups. To avoid a feeling of being underground, light finishes are prioritised, and textiles and furniture add warmth and comfort.

These basement rooms link to a network of underground tunnels around the hospital complex, which will one day be opened up as a visitor route called the MindWalk.

A sculpture garden has also been added outside of the building.

Throughout the museum, the interiors are unified by what CF Møller called a "robust and relatively restrained" material palette that simultaneously differentiates between old and new.

New architectural elements, such as staircases and openings, are lined in oiled oak, chosen for its warmth and tactility.

CF Møller is a Danish architecture studio founded by Christian Frederik Møller in 1924.

Its other recent projects include a Finnish psychiatric clinic that embodies the principles of "healing architecture" and the overhaul of the spherical Avicii Arena in Stockholm to "ensure its relevance for decades to come".

The photography is by Kirstine Mengel.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen's editorial team has been trawling design weeks across Europe this month to seek out some of the best new furniture and lighting. Below, we've compiled ten favourites from London Design Festival, Helsinki Design Week, Currents and beyond.

Split Lamp by Jake Robertson
chosen by Amy Frearson, editor-at-large

"The wealth of design talent in London was made clear in the LDF exhibition With Limitations, hosted by London retailer Aram and design collective Design Everything, which featured objects by over 100 designers.

"A fruit-inspired floor lamp by Jake Robertson was one of the standouts. The Manchester-born designer realised that, by make three slices in the based of aluminium pipe, he could split it open like a banana peel to form a stand.

"A light bulb screws in the top of the top, resulting in a product made from very few materials and with zero waste."

Tilo chair by Llot Llov
chosen by Jennifer Hahn, design and environment editor

"There was an embarrassment of riches to be found at the 20th anniversary exhibition of Llot Llov, the institutional Berlin design studio run by Ania Bauer and Jacob Brinck.

"In a former 1900s window blind factory, which opened to the public for the first time in decades as part of Berlin's newly launched Currents festival, the duo showed off its Throw lamps with drape-it-yourself shades as well as wood-veneer furniture with psychedelic patterns created by salt.

"A personal favourite was the Tilo chair, made using a newly developed technique that involves blasting liquid pigments at wood and allowing them to diffuse naturally across the fibre like inkblots on paper."

Floor lamp by Wretched Flowers
chosen by Jane Englefield, design and interiors reporter

"New York designers Loney Abrams and Johnny Stanish are partners in work and life at the helm of their emerging studio, Wretched Flowers.

"The designers split their practice between making lamps and mirrors out of sharp, interlocking fragments of laser-cut metal; and beautifully textured lighting and wallhangings crafted from stainless steel chainmail, woven to reflect the style of American folk art tapestries.

"Among their distinctive pieces is this floor lamp, which was presented as part of the Studio Iron exhibition during London Design Festival (LDF).

"Shaped like an elongated version of Verner Panton's iconic 1968 Flowerpot lamp, the design was cloaked in the studio's distinctively woven chainmail and tapestried with a delicate selection of hand-beaded glass and gemstones. The result is a striking piece of lighting that looks as if it's been decked out in a unique style of bejewelled armour."

Lotus Table Lamp by Carlo Nason for Gubi
chosen by Jane Englefield, design and interiors reporter

"Danish brand Gubi has reissued the Lotus Table Lamp, a mouth-blown Murano glass masterpiece originally conceived by the late Venetian designer Carlo Nason in 1969.

"Loosely shaped like the upward curving petals of a lotus flower, the lamp shade is formed from individually blown pieces of glass supported by an internal chrome-plated steel structure.

"Nason was considered a pioneer of his time, who established his reputation by rebelling against Murano traditions, despite being born into one of Murano's oldest glassmaking families.

"This is evident in Lotus, which features the 'pulegoso' method developed in the 1920s. The process involves small air bubbles being blown into glass to create a distinctively speckled, semi-opaque finish that gives the bulb an extra warm glow."

Membrana lamp by Valeria Montero
chosen by Jennifer Hahn, design and environment editor

"To make the pre-Hispanic dish of mixiote, meat is marinated in a parcel that looks like baking paper but is actually a thin membrane peeled from the inside of an agave leaf.

"One day, while eating the dish, Mexican industrial designer Valeria Montero realised that the material's transparency and resilience would make it equally suited to diffusing light – and born was the Membrana lamp.

"Instead of taming them into submission, the leaves are simply stacked together to create a gloriously spiky lampshade that contrasts with the precise lines of the stainless steel base.

"At LDF, the original lamp (above) could be seen alongside a new vertical version, created especially for the Village Meeting group show organised by East London studio All Ears, which turned out to be one of the highlights of the festival."

Portal of Seedlings by Filippo Muzi Falconi
chosen by Jane Englefield, design and interiors reporter

"Italian-born, London-based artist Filippo Muzi Falconi transformed a disused domestic fireplace with the insertion of a ribbed wood mantelpiece.

"Muzi Falconi constructed the decorative shelf out of hollowed, rough-sawn pieces of white ash, which were planed and assembled with shouldered dovetail joints.

"The artist then used gouges to hand-sculpt the mantelpiece's pleasingly wave-like patterns that amplify the timber's naturally varied grain.

"Called Portal of Seedlings, the project is a beautifully creative way to transform a formerly defunct interior feature. The mantelpiece is among the 34-strong shortlist of buildings, furniture and objects nominated for a 2026 Wood Award."

Tracks lamps by WINT Design Lab
chosen by Jennifer Hahn, design and environment editor

"From its workshop in Berlin's defunct 1970s Tegel Airport, WINT Design Lab has proven that robots can do origami.

"Or more specifically, they can cut and score intricate patterns into paper, which can then simply be folded by humans to create the Tracks lampshades (top and above).

"Studio founders Felix Rasehorn and Robin Hoske, who showed the lights as part of the Seetech exhibition at Berlin design festival Currents, say the robotic fabrication enables on-demand production with every shade cut to order in a matter of minutes.

"But to me, the most impressive thing is how it underlines the ability of humble paper to bend light and shadow to its will."

Tyyne acoustic screen by Sistema for Niimaar
chosen by Nat Barker, features editor

"Launched this month at Helsinki design fair Habitare, the Tyyne acoustic screen combines two of Finland's favourite things: wood weaving and silence.

"Marketed as suitable for dividing spaces in residential, hospitality and office settings, it was designed by interior architecture studio Sistem for circular design company Niimaar.

"In a partnership facilitated by the Finnish innovation agency Sitra, the product uses strips of oak sourced as leftovers from Finnish luxury sailboat maker Swan. It's made entirely in Finland, with wood-fibre acoustic filling from Aisti."

Bad Posture Chair by Mara Bragagnolo 
chosen by Cajsa Carlson, editor

"If there are two things I like, it's all-wood furniture and geometrical, almost brutalist shapes, and designer Mara Bragagnolo combined both these things in her monolithic, aptly named Bad Posture Chair.

"Shown as part of the You Can Sit With Us exhibition curated by design duo 2LG, the chair was designed to draw attention to the fact that many people – especially neurodivergent people – sit in ways that aren't supported by traditional seating.

"Bragagnolo created three chairs in total, one of which was shown during Shoreditch Design Week, designed to adapt to the recurring ways in which people sit.

"It may not look super comfortable, but its sculptural shape and sleek lines definitely made me want to take a seat."

Maille by EJM Studio for Collate Lobby
chosen by Amy Frearson, editor-at-large

"Chainmail seemed to be the material of the moment during this year's London Design Festival, with a few examples of this steel mesh on show across town.

"While most were fairly decorative, I was particularly impressed with how Edward Milton of London-based EJM Studio had found a more versatile use for this intricate metal cloth – as a minimalist partition screen.

"Launched as part of the debut collection from new editions label Collate Lobby, Maille is structured by a polished stainless steel frame. The chainmail slips over this frame like an off-the-shoulder dress, with just enough give that it flexes lightly when touched."

item.content:encoded:
British studio David Chipperfield Architects celebrates 15 years of the Hepworth Wakefield and Turner Contemporary in this short film, shared exclusively with Dezeen.

Opened within weeks of each other in 2011, the Hepworth Wakefield gallery in West Yorkshire and the Turner Contemporary museum in Margate are considered two of the studio's most important projects, influencing the evolution of its work that followed.

To mark their 15th anniversary, David Chipperfield Architects is publishing this short film exclusively with Dezeen, which documents the impact of the projects through insights from people who work at and frequent the galleries.

"This year marks the 15th anniversary of both Turner Contemporary and Hepworth Wakefield, two of our most important projects," the studio told Dezeen.

"Opening within weeks of each other, they represented something of a homecoming for the practice after years of success outside the UK."

Read:

Mary Duggan Architects reveals angular workshop for The Hepworth Wakefield Garden

"Fifteen years on, both museums have exceeded expectations," added David Chipperfield Architects.

"The projects share not only similar civic ambitions and timing, but also a formal approach: sculptural, monolithic responses to their settings, with a focus on natural light that would go on to influence our later work."

In the film, glimpses of the landmark projects are interspersed with numerous interviews, including one with Turner Contemporary employee Katie Barber. Barber said that the museum has triggered a creative renaissance in Margate, despite the local community's initial hesitation about the project.

"Turner Contemporary was conceived in the mid 2000s," she reflected. "Margate was going through a pretty low ebb; it started a bit of a creative resurgence."

David Chipperfield Architects was founded by David Chipperfield in 1985. Elsewhere, it recently transformed a historic Spanish bank into Faro Santander museum, and it is designing the red-brick Nobel Center in Sweden.

item.content:encoded:
Archtober, Design Week Lagos, Designblok and Design Week Mexico are among the key events featured in Dezeen Events Guide this October.

Other events taking place during the month include the Stirling Prize ceremony, Dutch Design Week, Design Miami Paris and Design Week South Africa.

Archtober
1 to 31 October, USA

Archtober is an annual architecture festival that takes place throughout the month of October in New York City.

The festival programme follows the theme In Our Hands, with exhibitions, talks, tours and screenings addressing resilient, inclusive and sensorial design.

Design Week Mexico
5 to 11 October, Mexico

This year, Design Week Mexico has chosen to honour Chile through its exhibitions and talks, reflected in the festival theme Perspectives from the Global South.

The week-long festival also hosts tours and fairs in Mexico City. Each year it also transforms a residential property into an indoor and outdoor immersive showcase.

Designblok
5 to 11 October, Czech Republic

Located at various venues in Prague, including the Prague Industrial Palace, the National Gallery Prague and the Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague, Designblok's festival programme spans exhibitions, awards and talks.

The 28th iteration celebrates a range of disciplines, including art, jewellery, fashion and product design.

The Design Talks 2026 programme is presented in partnership with Dezeen, and welcomes designers Lee Broom, Laurids Gallée and Daniel Rybakkenas speakers.

Design Week South Africa
8 to 25 October, South Africa

Design Week South Africa takes place over two separate weeks, hosting Johannesburg and Cape Town editions, with the former running from 8 to 11 October and the latter from 22 to 25 October.

The festival organisers have set the theme The Shape of Us for the events programme, focusing on local design, heritage and culture.

For four days, each city will be home to exhibitions, installations, open studios and showrooms, workshops, talks and tours.

Stirling Prize ceremony
15 October, UK

This year's Stirling Prize ceremony, hosted by The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), takes place at London's Old Billingsgate Walk.

The evening will celebrate the six architecture projects that are nominated for the award and announce the winner of the prize.

The shortlisted practices are Sergison Bates, Bennetts Associates, Mary Duggan Architects with RUFF Architects, Renzo Piano Building Workshop with Adamson Associates, Haworth Tompkins and Witherford Watson Mann Architects.

Dutch Design Week
17 to 25 October, the Netherlands

2026 marks the 26th edition of Dutch Design Week, which takes over the city of Eindhoven, spanning its galleries, studios, institutions and public spaces.

The theme for the latest edition is R.A.W., highlighting unpolished design in its rawest state. This is explored through exhibitions, workshops, seminars, film screenings, performances and parties.

The festival's events cover a range of topics, including ecology, care, inclusion, sustainability, education, liveability, digital, public, and personal.

Design Week Lagos
18 to 25 October, Nigeria

Design Week Lagos is an annual festival that spotlights pan-African design through exhibitions, talks and workshops.

This year, the festival addresses five key categories: design culture and systems; manufacturing, brands and trade; product, furniture and industrial design; interior design; architecture and the built environment.

Key events in the programme include the Made by Design trade show and the Design and Innovation Exhibition.

Design Miami Paris
20 to 25 October, France

Located at L'hôtel de Maisons, the Design Miami fair hosts its Paris edition, showcasing furniture and design objects from 20 global galleries.

The upcoming event explores the theme Design for Presence, which frames design as a means of connecting with others and staying present.

About Dezeen Events Guide

Dezeen Events Guide is our guide to the best architecture and design events taking place across the world each year. The guide is updated weekly and includes virtual events, conferences, trade fairs, major exhibitions and design weeks.

Inclusion in the guide is free for basic listings, with events selected at Dezeen's discretion. Organisers can get standard, enhanced or featured listings for their events, including images, additional text and links, by paying a modest fee.

In addition, events can ensure inclusion by partnering with Dezeen. For more details on inclusion in Dezeen Events Guide and media partnerships with Dezeen, email eventsguide@dezeen.com.

item.content:encoded:
With Britain's universities in dire straits, a radical rethink of how these institutions manifest as physical infrastructure is long overdue, writes Owen Hopkins.

University campuses are bustling once again, studios are hives of activity and lectures are in full swing.

It's a cycle that's been repeating for years, decades, centuries. And this is mirrored in the perennial nature of many of the debates around architecture and higher education.

Even in response to their own stated missions, universities as currently constituted would not be invented today

Is it too detached from the profession? Or is it vital to learn away from the mostly mundane realities of practice? Is architecture a creative discipline or a service industry?

The questions underlying the future of architecture in higher education are much the same as those facing architecture itself – and always have been. But in the UK at least, one big thing has changed in the last few years, and that's the threats universities are now facing not just to business as usual, but to their very existence.

Having bet big on high-fee-paying foreign students to plug funding shortfalls caused by rising costs and real-terms declines in home student income, in recent years universities have been stung by big drop-offs in the numbers of students prepared to come and study abroad. The resultant massive funding gaps at many universities have precipitated hastily conceived reorganisations – code for redundancies.

Read:

BIG designs "new kind of urban university" for Bentonville

But the threats universities are facing arguably run much deeper. It is fair to say that even in response to their own stated missions, universities as currently constituted would not be invented today.

In concept, they remain largely true to their medieval origins, cosplaying as 21st-century organisations infused with management speak. Despite efforts to "reach out" and forge greater links with industry and communities, they frequently still act as closed-off repositories of knowledge, training generations of students for yesterday's economy.

It is a characteristic of all institutions that once they reach a certain size and age, they shed their founding mission and exist simply in order to perpetuate themselves. And so it is with universities, with the transformations instigated by institutions across the country in response to the funding crisis really being about protecting the status quo.

The absence from universities of radical thinking around their future and fundamental purpose is little surprise

Amid all this, the absence from universities of radical thinking around their future and fundamental purpose is little surprise. What is surprising is the lack of comment, let alone ideas, from the architectural world given how the future of universities is an urban and ultimately spatial question.

Universities have long been core to successive governments' policies for regenerating Britain's post-industrial northern cities. In places like Leeds, Sheffield, Newcastle, even Manchester, universities have been positioned as "anchor institutions" – spurs of economic development, but also and arguably more critically among those cities' largest single employers.

Moreover, the expansion in student numbers during the 2010s has also led to the building of large amounts of student housing, transforming towns and cities up and down the country. If any one of the large urban universities went bust – which is not as unlikely as it seems – the effects for local economies would be disastrous, and arguably even worse than deindustrialisation.

Read:

"It is easy to find fault in architecture education"

This conception of universities as fundamentally spatial entities is hardly new, of course, and in particular was at the heart of a project that sought to reimagine the university for the post-industrial age by the iconoclastic architect and thinker, Cedric Price.

Published in 1966, Price's Potteries Thinkbelt project was conceived against the twin backdrop of the Robbins Report of 1963, which led to a massive expansion of higher education, and the country's impending shift from an industrial to a service-based economy, which was already having devastating effects on places like the North Staffordshire potteries – Price's chosen site.

What he proposed was nothing less than the dissolution of the distinctions between universities and places, education and industry, learning and everyday life.

The questions Price sought to address for higher education remain largely unanswered today

At its core, the Potteries Thinkbelt was a spatial proposition, turning the idea of a conventional university campus on its head. Making use of the rail lines that had been decommissioned in Beeching's railway cuts earlier in the decade, it re-conceived the university as a moveable network of modular classrooms, labs, technical centres, libraries, administration and accommodation.

The railway carriage was the basic modular unit, allowing spaces for teaching or research to expand or contract and to be moved around, and in the process, help reinvigorate the newly deindustrialised areas. The result was an anti-institution, a university imagined in a permanent state of flux, fluid and adaptable – and also quick to realise.

Prefiguring how residential development would become central to post-industrial regeneration in the 1980s and 1990s, housing – or "living units" as Price called it – was central to the project. But again, Price did things differently, using student housing not as an opportunity to make a quick buck as it is today, but as an experimental space in which to explore a range of new living patterns and typologies.

Read:

Can architecture's class of '25 crack the job market?

Whatever the model, common to all the units was their integration into the local community rather than existing as separate enclaves.

Ironically, as radical a provocation as it was, the Potteries Thinkbelt was soon superseded by an arguably even more radical idea that was actually implemented, with the founding of the Open University in 1969 as a massively decentralised institution enabled by emerging technology. Price, who was famously suspicious of building if it could be avoided, was no doubt pleased by this development.

But there's a further irony in that, despite the advent of the Open University, the questions Price sought to address for higher education remain largely unanswered today. Meanwhile, the possibility he saw of the UK "becoming an increasingly imbalanced community primarily involved in servicing other countries and providing facilities for hardy historiophile holidaymakers" has more or less come to pass.

Price was firmly of the belief that the questions underlying the provision of education were architectural ones

For all his criticisms of architects, Price was firmly of the belief that the questions underlying the provision of education were architectural ones. But to answer them meant doing architecture in a fundamentally different way, breaking free from convention and self-serving agendas, abandoning the ingrained superficialities of tradition and becoming properly radical. It was a call that, despite Price's provocations and personal charisma, has largely gone unheeded.

Today, the situation is arguably ever more urgent. Amid the rise of AI, economic stagnation, deepening regional disparities and consequent political extremism, the lack of radical thinking from universities is both extraordinary and entirely predictable.

But the same could also be said of architecture, which, has retreated from daring to posit anything approaching the scale, ambition or intellectual clarity of Price's proposition.

Read:

Five ways that architecture education needs to change

While Price's ideas are undoubtedly specific to a time and place, and his answers are not the ones we need today, the underlying principle of a university as a platform for continuous education, light touch in physical infrastructure, that connects culture and technology, a sense of belonging with economic endeavour, is more important than ever.

But, as Price himself noted, to reinvent higher education in anything like this way requires architecture to reinvent itself too.

Owen Hopkins is an architecture writer, historian and curator. He is the director of the Farrell Centre at Newcastle University. Previously he was senior curator at Sir John Soane's Museum and architecture programme curator at the Royal Academy of Arts. He was also part of the curatorial team for the British Pavilion at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale. He is the author of eight books, including Lost Futures: The Disappearing Architecture of Post-War Britain (2017) and Postmodern Architecture: Less is a Bore (2020).

item.content:encoded:
Start-up Freckle has created an AI-powered mobile phone for kids, designed around exploration to provide a break from parental restrictions and surveillance.

Developed with design studio Body Shop and targeted at kids aged seven to 13, the Freckle phone has features that encourage kids to spend time outdoors and observe the natural world, alongside more expected communication features like texting and calling with approved contacts.

There is no social media, web browser, app store or anything that could commonly be considered addictive. Instead, there is a suite of new features on its custom ClayOS operating system that are designed to appeal to kids without being unputdownable.

A Quests app lets kids go on ready-made or parent-invented missions, such as finding five different bugs in the park, while a Discovery Camera lets them take photos and find out information about the insect, animal, plant or object they've snapped.

Other apps are centred on story creation and answering kids' questions, while practical features like kid-friendly maps and payment through pre-loaded credit to let them navigate neighbourhood walks and bus trips on their own.

There's also a simple music player and that eternal childhood favourite: walkie-talkie mode.

Freckle was founded by Sam Terris, who previously founded plant-based food company Simulate, and its backers include Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian and his venture-capital firm Seven Seven Six.

The particular problem Terris wanted to solve is the lack of independent activity for kids, which denies important developmental experiences of exercising agency, managing risk and problem-solving.

"There's this huge chasm between what we think would really help a kid thrive and self-actualise in today's society and the actual infrastructure designed to do that," said Terris, who began thinking about Freckle while his wife was pregnant with their first child.

"We've seen that this loss of independence for kids is a primary driver of a lot of the anxiety and depression that these younger kids are facing today. Freckle is really an exercise in what would it look like to actually create a device that empowers kids."

Freckle's features were developed extensively with kids, and have a look, feel and functionality that they find appealing. The quests and photo library, for instance, are like "a real-life Pokedex" to inspire collection, Terris says.

Read:

AI toys could stunt emotional development of young children, study warns

There are safety features and guardrails, but parents are encouraged to loosen the reins as much as kids are nudged to grasp them.

"Most products in this space are built around utility for parents, so they tend to over-index on surveillance and control," said Terris.

"We believe the best way to give kids more independence is to take them seriously. Right-sizing technology doesn't have to mean stripping it of joy."

Parents get an alert if their kid leaves a preset "safe zone", so parents do not need to constantly monitor their location, and they'll be informed if a child mentions a sensitive topic like bullying but won't receive a full activity log.

AI underpins several of the apps – all of which can be optionally removed – but there is no open-ended chatbot and it is not intended to be an AI "companion" of the kind that is sometimes criticised for encouraging over-attachment or limiting play.

Instead, there are three AI-powered tools with a narrow purpose and corresponding characters: a wizard that can answer questions, a classifier that uses computer vision to identify objects and critters, and a storyteller for building interactive tales with family or friends.

"It's really easy to set effective guardrails now," said Terris. "If they ask about anything that's not really information dense, the product basically always ushers them back to a parent or a friend. It's not really there to continuously talk about your day."

Freckle also promises that the company will respect children's privacy, with a policy that will require verifiable parental consent, limited windows for data retention, and a prohibition on data use for training AI models.

The company worked with a 3D animator on the character design, based on clay models, for ClayOS, and with Body Shop, a new studio whose founders' past projects include collaborating with Modem on the Dream Recorder and 1X on the Neo robot, for the industrial design.

Body Shop co-founder Calvin Lien told Dezeen that the phone's form factor evolved to fit ideas of outdoor exploration, with a rugged case and a lanyard to hang around the neck "like a pair of binoculars you take outside to explore".

Terris cited Apple's flawed but visually impactful phone case for the iPhone 5C and Crocs Jibbitz as inspirations for Freckle, which can be accessorised with charms, while Lien named "the grounded tactility of Play-Doh, the modularity of Lego, and patches and pins from girls and boy scouts" as additional references.

Freckle is launching initially in the US and expects to begin shipping units from December 2026.
