item.content:encoded:
Thomas Heatherwick's campaign Humanise has embarked on a £1.5 million research project that will explore how the UK's streetscapes can be beautified to improve wellbeing.

Titled Delivering Humanised Places, the research is a partnership made up of the University of Glasgow, funding agency UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and Humanise, which was established by Heatherwick in 2023.

As part of the £1.5 million research partnership, Humanise said it wants to "challenge the 'blandemic' of dull, soulless development" and improve the way the UK designs and builds its urban environments.

The research project will look into how buildings in the UK can promote health and a sense of pride and belonging, and the potential socio-economic benefits of doing so.

"We've spent decades designing buildings with a narrow definition of function"

Particular focus will be made on the external design of buildings and streets and the impact this has on people's wellbeing, which Heatherwick argued receives too little consideration.

"Buildings in our towns and cities are experienced by millions of us every year as we pass by, and profoundly affect how we feel, yet we've spent decades designing buildings with a narrow definition of function, led by efficiency and cost, and too much focus on the needs of the people who use them inside," he said.

Read:

"The tone in architecture is that the public is ignorant" says Thomas Heatherwick

"The experience for passersby has been street after street of characterlessness," Heatherwick continued.

"In this time when society is more fragmented than ever, characterised by an epidemic of loneliness, too little thought has been given to how the design of the outsides of buildings could benefit society more broadly."

Humanise to "turbocharge the creation of radically more human places"

Humanise said that, according to its own research, 76 per cent of people in the UK believe that the appearance of buildings affects mental health.

It plans to build upon existing knowledge to strengthen the evidence of how buildings affect people's wellbeing, and use this to help create spaces that are engaging and joyful.

The research will involve centring local voices and hopes to give communities more of a say in decisions that impact the places they live.

It also hopes to influence policy, offering resources to mayors and developers that will help them implement "humanised" design in regeneration and development projects.

"Human-centred design can help us create places with character and joy, that support our wellbeing and sense of belonging, and that people value for generations to come," said Heatherwick. "Places people love also last longer."

"Our ambition is to turbocharge the creation of radically more human, engaging and joyful places," he continued. "The opportunity to make meaningful change is massive, but it will only be able to begin with the deep understanding that comes from measuring."

Government's plan to build new towns "a rare opportunity"

The Delivering Humanised Places research project comes as the UK government works towards its plan to build new towns in England, which Heatherwick sees as a prime opportunity.

"Britain is preparing to build homes and communities on a scale we haven't seen for generations," he said. "This is a rare opportunity to ensure that the human experience is at the heart of what we build."

Read:

Artists sculpt Bland Castles out of sand for Heatherwick's Humanise campaign

Heatherwick launched his Humanise campaign in 2023 to put into action ideas outlined in his book Humanise, a Maker's Guide to Building Our World, one of which is putting "an end to boring buildings".

Writer Owen Hopkins criticised the campaign as "an incredibly reductive way of assessing the built environment", arguing that it fails to identify the causes of poorly designed architecture and the ways to tackle them.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a flesh-like installation where "body, material, object and environment" work in mutual dependency is among the innovative projects by students at the Royal Academy of Art, The Hague (KABK).

Also included is an installation informed by quantum physics and a project that explores the vulnerability of living organisms through sculpture.

Royal Academy of Art, The Hague (KABK)

School: Royal Academy of Art, The Hague (KABK)
Courses: BA and MA programmes in Art and Design
Department heads: Carl Johan Högberg, Antoinette Vonder Mühll, Lauren Alexander, Chantal Hendriksen, Lotte Sprengers, John Fleetwood, Anthony Faramelli, Herman Verkerk, Sanne Jansen, Gerrit Uittenbogaard, Janice McNab, Jasper Coppes, Shadman Shahid, Jonas Althaus, Hans Venhuizen, Niels Schrader and Erik van Blokland

School statement:

"The Royal Academy of Art, The Hague (KABK), is a space where students have the freedom and support to explore their creative potential, while keeping their individual discipline and ideas central.

"At the academy, classrooms function as laboratories where students experiment, and tutors stimulate rather than direct.

"Each tutor combines their role with a professional practice in the cultural sector, which is reflected in their teaching style. By graduation, students have developed the tools needed to establish and situate their own unique practice.

"KABK provides a wide range of workshops. Students can work with textiles, ceramics, wood and metal, master traditional printing techniques or explore the 3D Lab and experiment with 3D printing.

"Workshop tutors, who also have extensive professional experience, are on hand to turn the students' ideas into reality.

"During the Graduation Show 2026, more than 220 art and design works were displayed. The exhibition reflected both the personal and collective experiences of more than 220 international graduates during their time at the academy.

"The projects by bachelor's, master's and PhD students explored a wide range of social and contemporary themes, from sustainability to quantum physics."

Will We Align? by Irja Linnerud

"Will We Align? is an installation inspired by quantum communication. It invites us to explore an unknown system. Light is being used as a visual language for relationships and directions.

"In this installation, the two central light sources are entangled: when one changes, so does the other. This behaviour is inspired by quantum entanglement, a phenomenon that challenges our everyday understanding of connection, and forms one basis of emerging quantum communication technologies.

"The work uses these principles as a starting point for a broader question: how do we engage with technologies and systems that are difficult to see, understand or influence?"

Student: Irja Linnerud
Course: Bachelor Interactive Media Design

Aftermarket by Jamie Smith

"This year, almost 750,000 used vehicles were no longer able to meet road standards or were simply no longer desirable.

"These cars are being shipped to Africa, and more than half of them will come from Europe. Aftermarket follows this journey.

"Through repairs, paperwork, bureaucratic offices and the repurposing of this consumer surplus, these vehicles are transformed in preparation for their new lives.

"As European governments wash their hands of the old and embrace the new, the question of who bears the responsibility for what was arises. How complicit are we in existing structures of global trade?"

Student: Jamie Smith
Course: Bachelor Photography

Negotiating the Grid by Simcha Ziya Moïse

"This project explores image-making changes when it begins from a pre-existing structure rather than an empty surface.

"Using a single element – the circle – within different grid systems, the work examines how variation, repetition, layering and sequence influence the relationship between structure and form.

"The grid is treated not as a neutral background, but as an active participant that shapes decisions and redistributes authorship within the making process.

"The resulting works emerged through an ongoing negotiation between structure and intervention."

Student: Simcha Ziya Moïse
Course: Bachelor Graphic Design

Between Reins and Teeth by Anahita Karimi

"Between Reins and Teeth investigates the vulnerability of humans and animals through garments, living organisms and sculptural installation.

"Challenging the illusion of human superiority, the project dissolves the boundaries between species and positions the body as a site of interdependence.

"Rather than presenting the human as separate from or dominant over the natural world, the work explores coexistence through relationships of dependence, care, exposure and transformation.

"Through fashion, installation and material experimentation, the work invites viewers to reconsider their relationship with the more-than-human world not through dominance, but through empathy and recognition of our fundamental interconnectedness."

Student: Anahita Karimi
Course: Bachelor Textile and Fashion

Soft Fence by Alexandria Liiv

"What's it like to share a space? How does personal space shape our interactions? How do bodies negotiate the tension between separation and connection?

"The project draws from my experience of growing up around wired garden fences and translates their logic into shared environments, reinterpreting their qualities through reclaimed mattress foam.

"By turning a rigid structure into something soft, it creates a permeable threshold that suggests privacy, marks personal space without diminishing openness or becomes a point of encounter and connection.

"Soft fence questions fixed boundaries, proposing instead emotionally responsive physical limits that shift alongside human relationships."

Student: Alexandria Liiv
Course: Bachelor Interior Architecture and Furniture Design

Inklinking by Ruben Dijkstal

"Inklinking is a kinetic sound installation that takes inspiration from the slow sinking and shifting of everyday brick streets.

"Suspended between the architecture above and the soil beneath, the work functions as a membrane that responds to subtle forces, continuously oscillating between deformation and reordering.

"Through movement and sound, the installation explores how systems that appear stable are constantly shaped by gradual processes of change.

"Small shifts accumulate over time, unsettling the grid and revealing the fragile balance between order and entropy."

Student: Ruben Dijkstal
Course: Bachelor ArtScience

Beyond the Horizon and Below the Waterline by Claire Robin Santen

"Europe's tallest structure is practically invisible. Standing 472 metres tall on the seabed in the North Sea, the Troll A platform is taller than any building on land in Europe. It extracts oil and gas.

"'Beyond the Horizon and Below the Waterline refers to the boundaries that mark the limits of our knowing.

"The footprint behind these limits is not immediately visible, yet man-made structures occupy the sea, extracting resources that become our energy and plastics.

"The work translates this invisibility through video and a sound-transducing steel platform below your feet. It asks: how can something so vast remain unseen?"

Student: Claire Robin Santen
Course: Master Non Linear Narrative

Gallery Zero by Stella Kechagioglou

"In the institution in which everyone has a space, where is the place for the common?

"Gallery Zero is the first self-organised common space within the Royal Academy of Art, The Hague (KABK). Developed in response to the absence of a shared space within the academy, the project explores how underused spaces, materials and social relations can be activated through collective participation.

"Rather than proposing a finished design, Gallery Zero functions as an evolving framework shaped by its users.

"Gallery Zero questions traditional notions of authorship and proposes a model of spatial production based on care, collaboration and shared responsibility."

Student: Stella Kechagioglou
Course: Master Interior Architecture

A Trace of Dinner by Zizi Mitrou

"Having conducted extensive research on the origin of glaze ingredients, I learned that their transportation requires a lot of energy. I began looking for an alternative.

"I realised that all I need to create a glaze is whatever is left on the table. I started reaching out to local restaurants and collecting and processing waste.

"Together with a few restaurants, I sought ways to create menus attuned to the possibilities for glazing. The aim was to create a dinner that was as zero-waste as possible, while the ceramics tell a story about the way we consume."

Student: Zizi Mitrou
Course: Master Industrial Design

Ladder by Gintarė Razmaitė

"The inspiration behind this project lies in Lithuanian wood carving, which is expressed through the intentionally abstracted shapes of diacritics connected to their base letters.

"This approach allows the typeface to be set in large, multi-line headlines without diacritics disrupting the rhythm of the composition.

"Floral ornaments inspired by the Lithuanian tradition of foraging introduce an illustrative layer to the display style.

"The accompanying text typeface is a lighter, more rationalised interpretation of the display design, optimised for reading at smaller sizes.

"Together, they form a versatile type family for a wide range of applications."

Student: Gintarė Razmaitė
Course: Master Type and Media

Litany for a Failing Machine by Priyageetha Dia

"Built around a voice delivering a sermon assembled through a language model's text-prediction process, Litany for a failing machine is an installation that examines the convergence of sonic governance, voice-cloning ethics and end-times rhetoric.

"The work considers how prophetic speech and automation converge within a contemporary colonial matrix of power – the interlocking control of knowledge, authority and language in the datasets and predictive logics from which machine speech is assembled.

"The work attends to how artificial intelligence inherits and amplifies older regimes of epistemic domination, and how statistical prediction acquires the sonic register of belief."

Student: Priyageetha Dia
Course: Master Artistic Research

Fabricated Fears by Fenna Jensma

"Fabricated Fears is a counter-offensive against the visual regimes of far-right politics, and a plea for developing visual literacy.

"I unpacked innocent-looking images that are circulated within two far-right Dutch political parties. These images serve as sedatives, stripping away critical viewing and manipulating the viewer toward radical ideologies.

"Far-right politics is intertwined with the regulation and control of femininity. The 'protection' of (white) femininity is a familiar instrument of state violence.

"My work is based on the understanding that when the image of the 'innocent' white woman is propagated, all women's rights come under pressure and racist violence increases."

Student: Fenna Jensma
Course: Master Photography and Society

Maintenance is Maintenance is Maintenance is Maintenance by Roni(a) Johansson

"Performance and installation form a temporary climate in which body, material, object and environment enter relations of mutual dependency.

"Water functions as both material and infrastructure, continuously altering the conditions of the work through melting, saturation, drying, corrosion, evaporation and accumulation.

"Rather than representing maintenance, the work produces conditions that make maintenance necessary.

"The body does not direct the system but exists as one of its components. It is reorganised by the same material conditions it responds to: carrying, drying, wetting, waiting and repeating."

Student: Roni(a) Johansson
Course: Bachelor Fine Arts

item.content:encoded:
Local studio Prim Estudio has designed a white house with a balcony inset into an asymmetrical zinc roof and arched windows for contemplating the landscape outside Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Known as Los Tigres, the 187-square-metre house sits on an expansive property in Villa Rosa, on the banks of the Luján River. Set on a rough-hewn stone foundation, the house is elevated above the surrounding field, which floods multiple times per year.

The rectangular plan is oriented on an east-west axis with an extended southern wall to break up wind that carries across the plains. The house is just beyond trees that hold stables, barns and storage sheds for the property's agricultural activities.

To fit with the vernacular architecture of the existing buildings, Prim Estudio opted for a contemporary version of an agrarian form to meet the client's request for a relaxed, landscape-focused space.

"This was the most important premise for the studio: to create a space for contemplating the surroundings," the studio told Dezeen.

"It was one of the main design guidelines for the house and each of its spaces, ensuring that it would be consistent with the expansive landscape of the plain while remaining a structure of modest dimensions."

A load-bearing masonry system of aerated concrete blocks forms the perimeter wall, broken by red-toned wooden window frames and topped with high-density polyurethane insulation panels and corrugated zinc roofing.

The western end of the house is a large open-air covered patio that doubles as a garage and gallery-like barbecue space. It opens into the main living, kitchen and dining room.

A wood-burning fireplace and curved wooden bench complement the main window.

Read:

Estudio Futuro renovates compact Argentinian home around terracotta-paved patios

"Undoubtedly, the house's contemplative spirit is expressed through the large, segmental-arch window that dominates and balances the composition, highlighting the simple geography of the surroundings as viewed from within," the studio said.

"To achieve a cohesive composition, other spaces were designed that also function as vantage points: the loft on the upper floor and a small bedroom look out through porthole windows, while maintaining a shared architectural form."

Three bedrooms and two bathrooms form the eastern side of the house, separated from the public spaces by an inset covered patio and a sculptural staircase.

"To achieve a sense of vertical space, a staircase leads to the loft and the north-facing terrace, which serves as a vanishing point toward the outdoors, offering a sweeping view of the sky and the horizon," the studio said.

Locally sourced wood with a simple, unpretentious aesthetic pairs with red ceramic floors and pops of green in the kitchen cabinetry and exterior shutters to reinforce the vernacular identity of the house.

"The project is based on a stereotomic concept for the building's design – a heavy, massive, stony architecture that sits on the ground as if emerging from it," the studio said.

"Within this massiveness, openings are created to let in light. Through this precise act – using a lowered arch – the design frames an expansive, uninterrupted horizon that, if not framed as a 'landscape,' might feel oppressive or monotonous."

"Ultimately, the house succeeds in providing a sensitive and secure framework for an extreme and hostile environment."

White painted houses carry through the Argentinian landscape, reflecting the climate's strong sunlight.

Other recently completed designs include a compact home with terracotta patios by Estudio Futuro, a stilted modular house by SET Arquitectura and a guesthouse with insulation made of discarded sheep wool by DUB Arquitectura.

The photography is by Javier Agustin Rojas.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a proposal for sustainable urban settlements in the Atacama Desert is among projects from students at Tulane University.

Also featured is a project focusing on the preservation of historic buildings across the US Gulf Coast region, and a community-oriented proposal for affordable housing, healthcare and co-working facilities in New Orleans.

Tulane University

Institution: Tulane School of Architecture and Built Environment
Courses: Graduate studios and courses in Architecture, Historic Preservation, and Real Estate Development
Tutors: Fallon Samuels Aidoo, Alex Barthel, Liz Camuti, Rubén García Rubio, Adam Marcus, Cristóbal Molina Baeza, Mark Rabinowitz, John Renne and Heather Veneziano

School statement:

"Located in the heart of the US Gulf Coast, the Tulane School of Architecture and Built Environment is redefining the role and capabilities of architects, designers, urban planners, real estate developers and preservationists.

"The school offers a wide range of undergraduate and graduate academic programmes in architecture, design, historic preservation, landscape architecture and engineering, real estate development, and social innovation and social entrepreneurship.

"In addition to its individual, directed research and specialised electives, a key feature of the school is its research studios. These focus on a single topic, place or phenomenon over three years, delving into greater detail and complexity during each cycle.

"Each studio works toward the production of scholarly outputs such as books, monographs, articles, symposia and exhibits. Students have the opportunity to select several of these studios during their time at Tulane."

Group project: Preservation Studio II – Latrobe's on Royal

"The Preservation Studio II concentrates on documenting, analysing and planning for the preservation of built environments as a basis for understanding the technical, theoretical and procedural aspects of urban conservation.

"The studio includes intensive study of representative historic structures and landscapes, including streetscapes in New Orleans and Puerto Rico, where students work both as independent researchers and in teams to learn professional preservation concepts and methods.

"This Spring 2024 studio explored documentation and interpretive methods for Latrobe's on Royal and resulted in a Historic Structure Report (HSR) for the site, which also included information regarding recommended repair, rehabilitation and restoration procedures.

"Latrobe's on Royal is listed on the National Register of Historic Places under the name Louisiana State Bank. The structure is also designated as a contributing property within the Vieux Carré Commercial District.

"The building is significant for its association with architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe, who was coined the "father of American architecture". Its architectural style, contribution to the historic urban fabric of the French Quarter and role in the development of bank typology further contribute to its historic significance."

Students: Allyson Hinz, Bailey Godwin, Catherine Restrepo, Dang Doan, Eileen Tomczuk, Emily Stood, Isabel Coletti, Jenna Voss, Jessica Triche, Katherine Schwab, Kristian Carroll, Lauren Vagts, Lisa Black, Madeline Wilson, Maria Gabriela Arrieta Vallerino, Parker Heitzmann, Rachel Shannon, Sam Crowley and Tahlor Cleveland
Course: PRES 6042 – Preservation Studio II, Spring 2024
Tutors: Heather Veneziano and Mark Rabinowitz

Group project: Ecological Tectonics: Architectural Ceramic Assemblies for Climate Adaptation

"This research studio explores ceramic material assemblies as a site for architecture's ecological agency.

"Projects work across three scales: small material prototypes, domestic architecture and the ecosystemic scale to combine pragmatic questions of fabrication and assembly, with social and ecological questions about how architecture can adapt to a changing climate.

"Research at the material scale focuses on the production of 3D printed ceramic components and how these systems might open up new forms of ecological performance at an architectural scale.

"Working in teams, the students focused on alternative approaches to domesticity and how the building's envelope could modulate climate control, assist with water management and provide habitats for species of plants and animals.

"This repositions the building envelope – traditionally thought of as an impermeable barrier between inside and outside – as a deeper, thicker and more porous assemblage that actively negotiates the demands of structure, enclosure, privacy and habitat.

"It is in this negotiation that architecture's most elemental purpose – as a boundary and a device of separation – transforms into one of connection, kinship and ecological stewardship."

Students: Analiese De Saw, Caroline Cameron, Jacqueline Hemmen, Griffin Kass, Ariel Levine, Emma Lindley, Cassiana Mefrige, Clara Quandt, Caleb Schroeder, Emmet Tanzer, Alexa Trapani and Walter Workman
Course: ARCH 4042/6042 – Ecological Tectonics Research Studio, Spring 2025
Tutor: Adam Marcus

Group project: Preservation Studio I – Building Preservation

"The Building Preservation Studio concentrates on documenting, analysing and planning for the preservation of historic buildings.

"The studio includes multiple intensive studies of selected historic buildings and environments within New Orleans and the greater Gulf Coast region.

"The studio explored the differences between building stabilisation, adaptive reuse, rehabilitation and restoration.

"Local and non-local field trips exposed students to a range of historic structures, their ideal treatments from a preservation perspective and an opportunity to document historic environments and building conditions.

"In-class seminars covered hand drafting, teaching of specific graphic and drafting software, geospatial analysis and research techniques.

"Working in a studio setting, students produced measured drawings and illustrated research documents portraying historic buildings, materials and systems analogous to course assignments.

"Digital documentation and related presentation skills were developed over the semester, culminating with the final project and required submission of a studio portfolio."

Students: Emily Morris, Laura Neises, Tatiana “Chai” Paden, Lydia Desormeaux, Karina Roca, Hayley Chung and Tyler Allen
Course: PRES 6041 – Preservation Studio I, Fall 2024
Tutor: Alex Barthel

Group project: Gulf Coast Climate Futures: Reclaiming Abundance in Texas' Golden Triangle

"The Gulf Coast Climate Futures research studios are a series of interdisciplinary design research courses that challenge students to reimagine working landscapes in the Gulf Coast region, spanning Houston to Alabama.

"Focused specifically on the Golden Triangle region – Beaumont, Port Arthur and Orange – the studio examined how former oil and gas infrastructures could be adaptively reused to support marginalised communities in adapting to climate change, while creating spaces of ecological abundance.

"Students collaborated with an environmental justice organisation in Port Arthur named the Community in Power and Development Association (CIDA) to ensure the projects addressed real community needs.

"The methodology integrated rigorous research with speculative visioning, requiring students to synthesise complex socio-ecological data into design proposals that were both locally impactful and regionally replicable. A four-day field trip to sites along the Louisiana-Texas border provided essential on-ground understanding of the study area.

"The studio employed a multi-scalar approach, bridging regional, landscape and architectural scales through speculative design scenarios."

Students: Michael Bell, Kris Hamilton, Ben Cornet, Kate Galvin, Chester Griffiths, Cassie Kadish, Ethan Miesler, Natalie Miller, Sig Peterson, Zach Rich, Cole Schwabacher and Kris Smith
Course: ARCH 4041/5051/6051 – Gulf Coast Climate Futures Research Studio, Fall 2024
Tutors: Liz Camuti

Group project: Sustainable Design and Planning – The Majestic Two

"This graduate-level course proposes a theoretical new development plan. The Majestic Two proposal envisions a mixed-use, community-focused development along a historic corridor in New Orleans.

"Rooted in the area's legacy of Black entrepreneurship and immigrant business, the project seeks to increase residential density while delivering affordable housing, co-working and healthcare provider spaces.

"The design emphasises external circulation and shared outdoor areas to enhance community interaction and quality of life, while maximising unit efficiency.

"Sustainability plays a major role, as the design integrates rooftop solar arrays, Tesla PowerWall battery systems, R45 insulations and water retention strategies such as bio-gardens and permeable pavements.

"Ultimately, Majestic 2 aims to weave together affordability, sustainability and social infrastructure."

Students: Nick Carroll, Olivia Cartner, Justin Gonzalez, Lawanda Jackson and Jed Manning
Course: SRED 6220 – Sustainable Design and Planning, Fall 2024
Tutor: Fallon Samuels Aidoo

Reverse Timeline: A Proposed Preservation Plan for the City of New Orleans by Lauren Vagts

"This proposed historic preservation plan for New Orleans' historic sites allows for a holistic preservation effort between local communities, preservationists, local, state and federal officials, as well as other experts who will work together to explore innovative ways for preserving the city.

"While the city of New Orleans acts as a culturally and historically rich epicentre unlike anywhere in the world, its geographical location is incredibly fragile and vulnerable to natural catastrophic weather and engineering events.

"Many historical district documents are outdated, historic records remain analogue and there has been little to no discussion of a historic preservation plan at local, federal or global levels. However, recommendations in this proposal plan incorporate tangible and intangible historic preservation.

"This plan differs from other historic preservation plans as it provides varying stages within a fluid timeframe to thoroughly document the city of New Orleans. With sea levels rising globally, this overall plan can serve as a learning tool for similar coastal cities.

"Additionally, this plan places emphasis on early deadline efforts to include phases of completion, community engagement, diverse planning commissions and workforce development to ensure optimal preservation and documentation efforts are achieved."

Student: Lauren Vagts
Course: PRES 6930 – Identity of Place, Fall 2024
Tutor: Heather Veneziano

Campus Rentals Plaza – A Proposed Student Housing Development by Alec Rovner

"This course centres on conducting an original investigation within a client-defined framework to gain new knowledge in real estate development.

"Students researched and analysed a real site, applying problem-solving and scenario planning techniques using UrbanFootprint and GIS to explore land use, zoning, financial feasibility and community impact.

"The course integrates zoning, financial modelling and innovative development strategies. Throughout the process, students engaged with professional mentors and clients to ensure their work aligned with real-world industry standards, gaining confidence in both presentation and client communication.

"This specific project, Campus Rentals Plaza, is a proposed mixed-use student housing development adjacent to Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge.

"The project responds to a growing demand for high-quality, purpose-built student housing that supports walkability, sustainability and academic life.

"The proposed development – situated on a 12-acre site – delivers 197 residential units and approximately 154,000 square feet of commercial space for retail, restaurants and offices."

Student: Alec Rovner
Course: SRED 6740 – Directed Research, Spring 2025
Tutor: John Renne

Group project: The Atacama Desert Project Research Studio (Saul A.Mintz Global Research Studio)

"This research studio focuses on one of the driest and most ecologically distinctive environments on the planet.

"The Atacama Desert's ecosystem supports nearly one million inhabitants and is crucial for key industries such as copper and lithium mining, renewable energy production, innovative agriculture and advanced astronomical observatories.

"While certain areas of the desert have experienced decades without rainfall, the effects of climate change, including unforeseen climatic events, a global rise in temperatures and the spread of desertification, make the site exceptional for testing innovative ideas to mitigate and adapt built environments.

"After travelling to the Atacama Desert in Chile, students researched and proposed improvements to urban settlements within this extreme ecosystem.

"Emphasising social equity, sustainability, ecological integrity and risk resilience, this research studio provided opportunities to face real-world challenges, to explore impactful solutions for sustainable development in extreme environments and to gain skills that can be extrapolated to similar contexts globally."

Students: Lindsay Bopp, Bella Davies, Andrew Hall, Tracy Jones, Madeline May, Andrew Audemard, Kate Burkhart, Alex Cohen, Camilla Greppi, Asha Hokanson, Max Kaplan, Megan Schlief and Daniella Tirse
Course: ARCH 4930/6930 – Atacama Desert Project Research Studio, Spring 2025
Tutors: Rubén García Rubio and Cristóbal Molina Baeza

item.content:encoded:
New York's Museum of Modern Art has exhibited Full Disclosure: The Edge of Information Design, curated by Paola Antonelli, which features information design from classic infographics to a project with missing memories created using AI.

On display in a windowed gallery on the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) ground floor, the exhibition has pieces from The Synthetic Memories Archive by Spanish research and design studio Domestic Data Streamers.

Hung on the wall, the Domestic Data Streamer's 2D works feature images generated by artificial intelligence (AI) using prompt texts from real people. These were based on reconstructed personal memories and are shown underneath the pictures.

The project aims to create an archive of these memories, but Domestic Data Streamers also takes a therapeutic approach, using the technology for people with trauma or dementia.

The work is part of Antonelli's expanded definition of information design, drawing from MoMA's archive. Many of the pieces were featured in her 2008 exhibition, Design and the Elastic Mind.

"[Information design] is not always about data sets acquired from a scientific or a statistical entity," Antonelli told Dezeen.

Works of statistics are also present in the exhibition – as in Laura Kurgan and Dan Miller's Two Sides of the Same Coin model that shows the geographic distribution of "human-associated microbes" on one side and more than 12,000 years of global land use on the other to depict biodiversity loss.

Antonelli said she wanted to show the investigative fact of information design in a time of heightened distrust of institutions.

She said she was especially interested in designers who make their own data sets, representing a "complete design".

"In this particular moment where our trust is vacillating every day, I wanted to show how you're right not to trust anybody, but at least you can follow a designer's, a journalist's, a politician's path – to see whether you agree with the end product or not," Antonelli said.

This investigative approach was seen clearly in London-based Forensic Architecture and Forensic Oceanography's film The Seizure of the Iuventa.

It depicts the team's efforts to use recreations and models, such as remote sensing, to aid an NGO rescue boat accused by the Italian government of smuggling.

Read:

"Data replicates the existing systems of power" says Pulitzer Prize-winner Mona Chalabi

While information design usually breaks down aspects of information into impactful and understandable clips, some of the objects depict scale and complexity in a more literal way.

Antonelli installed Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler's Calculating Empires in a side room of the space. Covering three walls, the work features icons and text tracing institutions and theories across the full scope of human culture and communication since 1500.

William Villalongo and Shraddha Raman's graphic work extends the data collected by WEB Du Bois on the African diaspora and the employment of African Americans into the 21st century.

Digital representations of New York Times interactive articles about the fire at Notre Dame and the Tulsa Race Massacre show the use of information design in digital media.

Most of the projects were digitally made. Exceptions include the ink-and-pencil Dear Data series by Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec, a series of postcards between the two data designers depicting elements of their everyday lives.

Antonelli aimed to show an array of takes on information design and said that the medium matters less than the information.

"The medium itself doesn't really matter," she said. "People can narrate data."

"It's about recognising the effort to explain complex information in a truly understandable way."

Antonelli has previously talked to Dezeen about how designers can help slow the decline of humanity due to climate change. In 2023, Pulitzer Prize winner Mona Chalabi spoke to us about how "data replicates the existing systems of power".

Images are courtesy of MoMA. 

Full Disclosure: The Edge of Information Design is on at MoMA from 27 September to 13 June 2027. Find more exhibitions, festivals and talks in architecture and design at Dezeen Events Guide.

Dezeen Showroom: elegance meets modularity in the Camelot seating system, created by architect Antonio Citterio and Italian brand Flexform.

A dignified frame and plump goose down-filled cushioning meet in the Camelot seating system, which was built to excel in both customisability and comfort.

The seating system combines a solid wood-and-metal frame with textile upholstery and optional leather wrapping on the cylindrical top bar, giving a sophisticated material mix.

Ample cushioning with an outer goose down layer adds to the luxurious feel, making the cushions bulge invitingly over the frame and inviting passers-by to sink their bodies into the seats.

Piping in either a contrasting or tone-on-tone colour finishes the upholstery, showcasing Flexform's expertise in custom tailoring.

Buyers can choose from a wide range of colours for the piping and main fabric and also from a selection of metals and premium woods for the frame, giving their seating unique personality to suit their interior.

item.content:encoded:
A skeletal frame of reclaimed timber surrounds the elongated form of Skroget, a community sauna and public deck in Norway designed by student architecture studio Rare Collectiv.

Overlooking the busy harbour of Båtsfjord, known as Norway's fishing capital, the structure was designed and built by 15 students from the Design in Context course at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

Named Skroget after the Norwegian word for hull, the 40-metre-long structure is modelled on the skeletal frame of a boat. It contains public seating areas, a sauna room and a terrace with a fire pit overlooking a rocky bank at the water's edge.

The design was developed collaboratively by the Rare Collectiv team, beginning with 15 individual proposals that were then discussed, developed and narrowed down to three designs, before a final vote.

"For us, the line where the sea meets the land was the most interesting part of the site, and we wanted to be able to connect the sauna experience close to the cold water so in future it is possible to create a bathing possibility," Rare Collectiv told Dezeen.

"Through the long building we created two sides – a rough waterside and a more protected side toward the land and south. Even with stronger winds, the walls provide shelter to enjoy the sun from the south," it added.

"Together, the wooden frames evoke the carcass of a fish, or, as suggested by the name of the project, the hull of a ship."

Almost the entire structure of Skroget was built with lengths of reused timber, sourced from a building recently dismantled by the local municipality.

Its defining feature is the row of nineteen timber portals, which have been angled towards the harbour to create a sloping roof that extends to shelter a walkway and seating area on the southern side.

Read:

Rezen transforms hotel stables in Australia into "raw and direct" wellness centre

This walkway links the more public entrance and fire pit to the west to the sauna at the eastern end, with the space in between housing changing rooms and showers.

"This concept of the continuous hallway allows visitors to explore the building without a dead end, but rather exit and explore a different space of the site," the team explained.

Contrasting with the predominantly reclaimed-wood structure, the 15-square-metre sauna was constructed from new wooden elements, with a dark brown wooden exterior and a pale birch interior.

For Skroget's external furniture, the team created a family of benches, tables and chairs with sloping seats and backrests designed to echo the building's angular frames.

Elsewhere in Norway, Rabagast Studio – led by students from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Trondheim – created a small timber sauna floating atop a lake in Innlandet.

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include a crystal-shaped structure in northern Sweden by Bigert & Bergström and Puusauna in Finland, which Jaakko Torvinen supported with a colonnade of tree trunks.

A monolithic grey-brick home in Northern Ireland and a skinny house in Kyoto are among the most popular houses featured on Dezeen this month.

Also included in our monthly roundup of our readers' favourite residences is a lime-rendered house in Mexico, a cross-laminated timber holiday home in Sweden and a home in India built alongside mango trees.

Read on to find out more about Dezeen readers' favourite houses this month:

House and Studio in Kyoto, Japan, by Tato Architects

Measuring four by 30 metres, local studio Tato Architects filled this narrow site in Kyoto with a skinny home and ceramics studio illuminated by two skylit voids.

Inside, zigzagging staircases and walkways connect the home's separate eastern and western wings, which are elevated over an expansive ground-floor studio.

Find out more about House and Studio in Kyoto ›

Tollymore, UK, by McGonigle McGrath

Belfast studio McGonigle McGrath set six staggered rectangular volumes into a steep bank to form this riverside house in Northern Ireland.

Grey brick walls were built atop a stepped plinth formed from board-marked concrete, while large windows and glass doors overlook the surrounding nature.

Find out more about Tollymore ›

Casa Amona, Mexico, by Colar

Perched beside a wooded hill in San Cristóbal de las Casas, Casa Amona is a two-storey home and studio wrapped in white lime-rendered walls.

The home was designed by local architecture studio Colar for a multi-generational family, with a stacked layout of rooms that function as independent units and an enclosed ground-floor living space that can convert into a bedroom without architectural intervention.

Find out more about Casa Amona ›

Pine House, Sweden, by Johan Sundberg Arkitektur

Pine House stretches across a forested landscape in southern Sweden with a low-lying cross-laminated timber structure arranged in a cross-shaped plan.

Swedish studio Johan Sundberg Arkitektur wrapped the three-bedroom holiday home with pine panelling that was left exposed and untreated to weather over time.

Find out more about Pine House ›

House Beyond the Mango Trees, India, by InLe Architect

Indian practice InLe Architects shaded the interiors of this home in Kerala with timber shutters and the cooling canopy of two large mango trees.

The entrance is positioned between the trees, which leads to an elongated dining room designed as the heart of the home, and an adjacent outdoor patio.

item.content:encoded:
British carmaker Vauxhall has updated its griffin emblem, which has been pared back and lost its flag for the first time.

The logo is the 13th iteration of the brand's logo, which has incorporated a griffin since 1915.

In the latest update, Vauxhall's previous flat logo introduced in 2020 was further simplified, with the griffin made more angular. In particular, the mythical creature's neck hair was simplified while its beak was closed.

For the first time in the logo's 121-year history, the flag depicting the letter V no longer forms part of the logo.

"The griffin emblem is instantly recognisable, with Vauxhalls seen on almost every street in Britain," said Vauxhall design vice-president Mark Adams.

"Having adorned our vehicles in different forms for more than 120 years, we wanted to retain its essential elements while streamlining it for the next generation of electrified vehicles."

The revamped logo will be presented next month at the Paris Motor Show on the Vauxhall STX Concept. It will then be used on all future production models.

According to Vauxhall, the simplified logo was designed to be illuminated on its future electric vehicles.

Read:

Bentley unveils "biggest change" to logo in 100-year history

"As the griffin is now illuminated on the front of our latest models, this simpler design also makes it clearer and easier to identify," said Adams.

"The new look is sharper, cleaner and fits perfectly with the next evolution of our bold and pure design language."

The original griffin logo, designed by an apprentice at the company Harry Varley, was the winner of a competition to create a badge for the emerging car brand in 1915.

Varley incorporated the mythical creature into the logo as a nod to the coat of arms of Sir Falkes de Bréauté, who in the 13th century became the owner of the land in London now known as Vauxhall. This is where the car company, which began as the Vauxhall Ironworks, was first established.

Other car companies that have recently updated their logos include Bentley, which revealed the "biggest change" to its logo in its 100-year history last year.

All imagery courtesy of Vauxhall.

item.content:encoded:
The Royal Institute of British Architects has paid £150,000 to its former president Alan Jones, settling a long-running legal dispute over its handling of his personal information.

The £150,000 payment was listed in a draft of the institute's annual financial report, seen by the British magazine Architect's Journal (AJ), which broke the news yesterday.

In the draft, the payment is listed as a "settlement agreement" to an "ex-officio trustee". The AJ ascertained that this was Jones.

Payment followed long-term legal dispute

The payment concluded a long-term legal dispute between Jones and the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), which was settled in 2025. It was sparked by the organisation's handling of personal information and allegations about Jones, which were leaked to the press in 2020.

RIBA has since stated that the organisation is "bound by its confidentiality obligations, which prevent further comment", AJ reported. However, it remains uncontested that the money was sent to Jones.

Read:

RIBA president Chris Williamson to give up architect title

Jones is a Northern Ireland-based architect and academic who became RIBA president in September 2019.

In early 2020, RIBA submitted a "serious incident report" involving Jones to the organisation's regulator, the Charity Commission, and the architect temporarily stepped down from his role as president. Details of this report were subsequently leaked to the media.

Jones returned to his role in June 2020 following an independent investigation by law firm Browne Jacobson, which cleared him to return to office.

Dispute caused by "unauthorised" disclosure of information

When the dispute was settled in 2025, RIBA said it regretted the "unauthorised" divulgence of information about its president.

"RIBA has reached a confidential settlement with the past president of RIBA, professor Alan Jones, in respect of his claim that information relating to him was not adequately protected and controlled by RIBA," RIBA chair Jack Pringle said at the time.

"RIBA regrets the fact that unauthorised leaks occurred and the harm that this caused professor Jones and his family."

Jones was succeeded as president of RIBA by Simon Allford in 2021. Allford was followed by Muyiwa Oki, and later today's president Chris Williamson.

Williamson, who is co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, recently caused a stir when giving up his architect title to draw attention to the "absurdity of the current regulatory framework" of ARB.

item.content:encoded:
A recyclable timber pavilion designed to mimic wildflowers is among the prototypes built by students at BuildFest 2026, shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Designed by students from Lehigh University and Syracuse University, Wildflowers uses custom-designed 3D-printed joints to connect timber columns in an X shape that resembles flowers. It can be disassembled for future use.

BuildFest is a 3-day event held on the historic grounds of the 1969 Woodstock festival

The joints are fixed with simple hex bolts that leave three small holes in each piece so they can be removed and reused without damaging the timber.

The installation was part of BuildFest 2026, the fifth edition. The event returned to the historic grounds of the 1969 Woodstock festival in Bethel, New York and focused on large-scale structures designed to be adapted, dismantled and reused.

The festival marks the first instalment of a three-year curatorial initiative titled Acts of Construction.

Called Act One: Staging, the 2026 edition explored how the structures can accommodate different uses, performances and configurations, with future editions set to reuse and transform them.

At the edge of the forest, Proscenium by the University of Idaho used stump and roundwood rejected by commercial timber milling alongside dimensional lumber.

A timber truss framed a raised stage and suspended curtain, creating a performance space among the trees that recalled the Grand Stage at Woodstock.

Contact Hi-Fi by Cornell University was informed by prefabricated roof trusses and was constructed from pallet wood diverted from waste streams.

The installation featured modular trusses that can be rearranged into 12 configurations, with interchangeable panels featuring sonic transducers and sound-responsive lighting to create a backdrop for performances.

Also by Cornell University was BaleWorks, an installation and infrastructural prototype made from straw bales held within modular timber frames.

The structure doubles as a composting porta-john, bringing together agricultural waste, construction and public infrastructure.

At the festival's pond, the team from the University of California, Los Angeles constructed a floating modular ramp named Flotilla.

The raft could be assembled into a single structure, separated into individual rafts or rearranged to create spaces for performances.

Suspended among the trees, Flying Buttruss by Syracuse University & Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute was constructed using lumber, hardware and LED lights reused from last year's BuildFest.

The illuminated timber truss was relocated from the festival's camping ground to the forest, where it was raised between the trees and accompanied by a small bench made from leftover timber.

Read:

Students construct timber pavilions at Woodstock site during BuildFest

At night, several pavilions and installations were used for live performances and light shows.

BuildFest brings together students and faculty to design and build timber pavilions and multimedia installations as part of the Bethel Woods Art and Architecture Festival.

The 2026 festival took place over five days, with the installations remaining open to the public through November in Bethel, New York.

The photography is by Breyden Anderson and Kevin Furguson

BuildFest Acts of Construction took place from 9 to 13 September in Bethel, New York, with all installations remaining open until November. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Snøhetta added tunnelling playgrounds to Sky House, the final of four clubhouses that make up its Pavilia Farm residential development in Tai Wai, Hong Kong.

Called Sky House, the clubhouse was designed as a playground and fitness centre for all ages and combines play spaces with workout areas for senior residences.

It joins the Tea House, Well House and Farm House clubhouses, which opened in 2022 and were designed as a series of shared community spaces for a Hong Kong residential development centred around an urban farm.

An outdoor children's playground invites residents to the two-storey Sky House. Slides and platforms at various heights create an undulating landscape that extends into the interior ground floor, where a children's play area, a classroom and a music room are located.

Here, children can explore tunnels inside the hilly playground.

The upper floor comprises lounge spaces, fitness facilities and outdoor exercise areas designed for senior residents.

A domed skylight doubles as a rope-climbing tower at the centre of the building and connects the two floors, allowing natural daylight to fill the interiors.

"By bringing together spaces for different generations under one roof, Sky House supports meaningful encounters and strengthens community ties through everyday life," said Snøhetta.

Snøhetta intended for Pavilia Farm to introduce a new model of residential living – beyond offering private apartments in densely populated urban environments – that would support residents throughout all stages of their lives.

"Pavilia Farm began with a simple ambition: to create meaningful connections between residents, nature, and Hong Kong itself," said managing director of Snøhetta Asia Richard Wood.

"In one of the world's densest urban environments, the project provides a shared green sanctuary, the project demonstrates how architecture can shape relationships as much as it shapes space," he continued.

The studio has now completed all four clubhouses. These are arranged along a green farm at the centre of the development that offers residents access to shared gardens, urban farming and wellness facilities, as well as meeting and recreational spaces.

Each was designed to closely integrate with nature and respond to the surrounding mountains and the Shing Mun River.

The Tea House was designed as a cantilevered pavilion that overlooks the surrounding terraced landscape.

It has two water elements that were designed to have a calming effect – an outdoor pool on one side of the building and a cascading waterfall on the other.

Read:

Snøhetta unveils "green lung" urban farm in Hong Kong

The Well House, which is directly connected to the Tea House, has a gym, spa, sauna, an indoor pool and a badminton court.

Its galzed facade was designed to blur the boundary between architecture and landscape and bring people closer to nature.

At the heart of Pavilia Farm is the Farm House, which has three kitchens and a communal dining table to invite residents to cook and share meals together.

The clubhouse also features a bespoke table system that is supported by a moving rail on the floor and lets tables be combined or divided, depending on the size of the gathering.

According to Snøhetta, Pavilia Farm's layout was designed to encourage discovery and interaction.

"Rather than functioning as isolated amenities, the four clubhouses create a layered neighbourhood within the larger residential development, encouraging discovery, interaction, and participation in community life," said Snøhetta.

"Taken together, the four houses form more than a collection of communal facilities. They create a rich network of destinations woven into daily life, supporting residents of different ages, interests, and lifestyles."

Elsewhere, Snøhetta has recently completed Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota, USA, as well as the extension of the Queensland Performing Arts Centre in Brisbane, Australia, wrapped in a rippling glass facade.

item.content:encoded:
British architect Norman Foster is set to deliver a keynote speech at this year's Dezeen Awards party, which will take place at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November.

In his address, Foster will focus on the future of architecture, drawing on his position as one of the most influential architects of his generation.

One of the world's most respected architects, Foster leads global firm Foster + Partners alongside serving as president of the Norman Foster Foundation.

He has had an immense impact on global architecture over the past 60 years, with early landmark projects including the HSBC Building in Hong Kong and London Stansted Airport.

He remains at the helm of the global architectural powerhouse as executive chairman, with more recent significant projects including Apple Park in the USA and the Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi. The architect recently unveiled the final designs for memorial statues and a glass bridge dedicated to Queen Elizabeth II.

Foster is also one of the most decorated architects in history, being awarded the RIBA Gold Medal, AIA Gold Medal, Pritzker Architecture Prize and Praemium Imperiale award, while three buildings designed by his studio have won the Stirling Prize – including, most recently, a project described as the largest stone building built in the City of London since St Paul's Cathedral.

His foundation, along with his eponymous institute for sustainable cities launched in 2024, are initiatives that both promote interdisciplinary thinking and research to help new generations of architects, designers and urbanists anticipate the future as well as educating the civic leaders of the future.

Foster joined the architecture judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026, alongside industry leaders Annabelle Selldorf, Daniel Libeskind, Ma Yansong and Amanda Levete, judging this year's projects which came from over 90 different countries across the globe.

Last week, Dezeen revealed all 392 shortlisted projects in the running for this year's awards. The architecture shortlist was announced on Monday, the interiors shortlist on Tuesday, followed by the design shortlist.

Read:

Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind join Dezeen Awards 2026 master jury in London

Readers can now choose their favourite shortlisted projects to be awarded in this year's public vote.

Amongst this year's shortlisted projects are a mosque with a perforated, blanket-like roof of stone-clad steelwork, an over-century-old dockside warehouse conversion and a modular furniture system made up of upholstered squishy balls.

Dezeen will announce the public vote winners and across social media channels ahead of the party on 16 November.

Tickets for the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are on sale. The occasion is an opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work.

Dezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a lamp crafted from volcanic stone and informed by a sunrise is among the projects from Instituto Tecnológico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey.

Also featured is a stone plate with a glass cloche referencing Mexican cinema, and a wooden stool featuring leather tassels.

Tecnológico de Monterrey

School: Architecture, Art and Design
Showcase: Inédito Universitario 2026 at Design Week México
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

School statement:

"In Mexico, black has been matter before pigment, an ancestral tradition in which colour is born from origin or from fire.

"Black takes up that heritage through contemporary design, with pieces whose tone comes from the material itself: black clay, volcanic stone, marble, charred wood and ceramics.

"As part of Design Week México, thirteen pieces, by design students at Tecnológico de Monterrey, were developed alongside artisans and workshops from different regions of Mexico.

"The exhibition core is monochromatic: every object is read through its form and the trace of the process that turned it black."

Estrato by Mariana Gayón García

"Estrato is a tabletop book organiser made of black volcanic stone that links the memory of the earth with the knowledge held in books.

"The design draws on the stone's natural qualities (weight, texture and density), turning them into part of its function of holding and organising books.

"The piece comes from understanding matter as memory. Volcanic stone carries the history of the land, and its black colour evokes the wisdom and knowledge inherited from earlier generations.

"That material memory meets the intellectual memory held in books, bringing materiality, memory and knowledge together in a functional, contemporary object."

Student: Mariana Gayón García
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter

Tatemada by Gabriela Covarrubias Rodríguez

"Tatemada is a table lamp made of black clay from Oaxaca that brings artisanal pottery together with contemporary design, turning a traditional material into a decorative lighting object for interior spaces.

"Inspired by Oaxaca's traditional smoke kitchens, the piece reinterprets the trace that fire and the passage of time leave on objects and the spaces they inhabit.

"Its rough finish evokes the soot that builds up on surfaces, while the warm light emerging from its openings stands for the warmth of a wood fire."

Student: Gabriela Covarrubias Rodríguez
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Comitl by Lucía Gallegos Bátiz

"Comitl is a decorative vessel inspired by the shape and structure of the cuexcomate, the ancestral structure used to store corn.

"Its silhouette draws on the essence of these ancient corn containers and reinterprets it for the present day. The rounded body extends into a conical section, creating a contrast between textures and elements.

"The piece seeks to recover and reinterpret the design, knowledge and forms of ancient Mexico from a contemporary point of view."

Student: Lucía Gallegos Bátiz
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Inframundo by Juan Pablo Castillo Villalón

"Inframundo starts from the colour black, understood not as a finish, but as the natural outcome of a material process.

"In the Mesoamerican worldview, black was linked to the underworld: a sacred space of transition where darkness did not signal an end, but the origin of transformation, life and rebirth.

"Working from that idea, the piece is a ceramic set made up of a cup and a filter for preparing cacao. Joined together, the two pieces evoke the silhouette of a pre-Hispanic vessel, and their geometry – divided into three sections – represents the underworld, the world of humans and the celestial world.

"The black colour emerges naturally during firing through glazes with natural pigments and reduction reactions, making the transformation of the ceramic visible.

"More than a utensil, the piece proposes a contemporary ritual for preparing cacao, inviting people to rediscover this ingredient with respect for its origin."

Student: Juan Pablo Castillo Villalón
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Veda by Emanuel Reyes Díaz

"Veda is an appetiser plate that uses a frosted glass dome to progressively cover and reveal the food arranged on a volcanic stone base.

"The piece takes as its reference the way censorship in Mexican cabaret cinema (cine de ficheras) concealed certain images, leaving room for fantasy and desire.

"The device is carried over into the act of eating, drawing a parallel between desire and appetite through anticipation, reveal and enjoyment."

Student: Emanuel Reyes Díaz
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Bartola by Alejandra Arnaud Escobar

"Bartola is a stool inspired by cowboy aesthetics and guided by the Japanese philosophy of conscious use of resources, built in purpleheart wood, leather and brass fittings.

"The piece revalues traditional crafts – carpentry, leatherwork and jewellery-making – bringing them together in a contemporary object that puts materiality, craft and permanence first.

"According to its own author, Bartola rests on three core ideas: craft, because it seeks to revalue traditional techniques; material, because the materials are the protagonists of the design; and character, because every detail is meant to communicate identity and permanence.

"The piece aims to become a statement object, capable of showing that furniture can preserve crafts, reinterpret traditions and create meaningful experiences."

Student: Alejandra Arnaud Escobar
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Bucle by Paulina Ibarra Gutiérrez

"Bucle is a modular shelving system built around a crocheted wire panel, scaling jewellery-making processes up into functional, contemporary furniture.

"The piece does not treat manual work as a disadvantage against industry, but instead challenges its historical devaluation as domestic labour.

"By bringing it into contemporary design with a high level of technical rigour, it becomes a statement of exclusivity, intentionality and precision."

Student: Paulina Ibarra Gutiérrez
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Rastro by Tamara Cagigal Esclusa

"Rastro is a modular system made of two charred-wood pieces that, combined, generate different patterns and compositions for cladding or decorating walls.

"Its reliefs evoke the textures of cooling lava, and the contrast between geometry, texture and materiality turns each composition into a surface that transforms the space.

"The piece grows out of the idea that transformation does not disappear, but remains as a trace. It interprets the solidification of lava through charred wood, carrying the memory of a process of change into a new material."

Student: Tamara Cagigal Esclusa
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

El Resguardo – Teresa, Carola and Lidia by Anabella Cariño Olivier

"El Resguardo is a family of three containers – Teresa, Carola and Lidia – made of black Tecali marble with charred maple lids.

"The collection combines the weight, shine and permanence of stone with the warmth of a wood transformed by fire, in soft, compact forms meant for keeping personal, everyday objects.

"The project starts from the act of keeping close what we choose to hold on to. It explores the contrast between two dark materials: marble, mineral and polished, which reflects light; and charred maple, organic and transformed by fire, which absorbs it.

"The natural variations in grain and tone of each block of marble are kept as evidence of the material's origin and of each piece's craft process."

Student: Anabella Cariño Olivier
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Tlecuil by Sophie Nicole Aguilar Ramírez

"Tlecuil is a table lamp that holds a sunrise. A crater carved into a volcanic stone base is where the light lives.

"The bulb barely peeks out from its upper half, like a sun rising between mountains, and a hand-dyed cotton cloth shade fades from black to ochre, letting that first glow escape.

"The name comes from the Nahuatl word for hearth, the hollow where fire is kept. The piece draws on the Legend of the Suns, in which Nanahuatzin throws himself into the hearth, and his sacrifice lights the fifth sun.

"With that, it proposes black not as absence or death, but as the origin from which all light is born. Darkness is the condition for fire to exist, and fire the condition for light to exist."

Student: Sophie Nicole Aguilar Ramírez
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

item.content:encoded:
North American football league Major League Soccer has moved its New York headquarters to the Penn 2 skyscraper and commissioned US studio TPG Architecture to have it mirror the dynamics of a soccer pitch.

The office opened earlier this year just before the 2026 FIFA World Cup, which also coincided with the thirtieth anniversary of the Major League Soccer (MLS) organisation and football's "surging cultural momentum", according to TPG Architecture.

The two-storey office integrates elements from a football stadium, according to the studio, such as an entrance area that resembles the tunnel players run through to enter the field.

"The 'office as a stadium' concept emerged from feedback the MLS Commissioner had collected from current and former players, coaches, retired athletes, and long-standing employees about what they hoped to see in the new headquarters," said the studio.

"The architectural layout mirrors the dynamics of a soccer pitch, utilising fluid curves inspired by the physics of a moving ball and the momentum of the game to inform how the space is experienced."

Visitors enter through the tunnelled elevator bay clad in custom mesh weave that is "goalie net-esque". LED lighting behind the walls and ceiling-mounted LED screens can be programmed to display branding for visitors, clubs, or sponsors, according to the studio.

This space leads into a reception area, and beyond that, a double-height lobby is centred around a grand staircase. A wall of jerseys surrounds one side of the reception area, while the Championship Cup is displayed on a pedestal on the other.

The grand staircase connects to spaces such as meditation and wellness rooms, coffee bars and a bottom-floor cafe that are together referred to as the Midfield, or a central space where employees can gather and interact.

The staircase itself is lined with a digital LED banner that represents different tiers of a stadium, and flashes players and branding.

At the bottom level, the floors open up into the cafe area and a "dugout-style" IT technical corner that takes cues from the technical area of a stadium, where coaches gather during a game.

Read:

HOK unveils Major League Soccer's first fully electric stadium in Queens

Elsewhere, conference and meeting rooms are lined with screens and primarily grey carpeting and seating. Bold "grass green" and cobalt "MLS-blue" tones were also used across furniture and accents.

Employee working floors are lined with a patterned carpet and desk units.

The studio said it incorporated a diagonal slash motif throughout the project, pulling from the MLS shield logo, which features an elongated slash across its centre.

TPG Architecture also completed a headquarters for the NHL in Manhattan and the office of an advertising agency in North Carolina.

The MLS is the primary football league in the United States and Canada and was founded in 1996 after the US hosted the 1994 World Cup.

Dezeen recently rounded up the 23 stadiums slated to host the 2030 World Cup.

item.description:
