item.content:encoded:
With AI driving demand, vast data centres are increasingly in the news as people question the impact on local environments. Can architects help to make these buildings look and function better?

When was the last time that buildings animated the population of the United States as much as the current wave of data centre development?

In the past two years, the huge, boxy buildings have provoked backlash across partisan lines as plans have been announced across suburban and rural America.

Housing the servers that power cloud computing and, now, artificial intelligence (AI), data centres are an important part of the infrastructure that supports the internet.

Usually located in sparsely populated areas, these nondescript buildings have been largely ignored as architecture, but this is beginning to change.

"Data centers are, in general, an example of poor design," Spanish academic Marina Otero Verzier, who won the 2022 Wheelwright Prize for her theories on data centres, told Dezeen.

With growing public awareness of data centres' heavy land, water and energy use, pushback has been intense. Nearly 70 per cent of the US population opposes their construction. Yet the US is set to double its data centre building to keep pace with the boom in AI, with spending on data centre infrastructure projected to top $800 billion per year globally in 2026.

Architects are largely absent from the trend – something that Otero Verzier believes needs to change if there is any hope of these structures being positive, or at least neutral, contributors to the built environment.

"Architects should be involved in the design of the building – from the materials used to the metabolic relations it establishes with the environment and communities – as well as in thinking about their public nature as repositories of collective knowledge and their broader urban and territorial planning," she said.

"Architects have a ton of value to add to the data center conversation"

So far, that hasn't happened, and even some developers recognise data centres have suffered from a lack of design thinking.

Daniel English, co-founder and managing partner of Legacy Investing, a real estate firm that specialises in data centres, believes that architects were sidelined in the early designs of data centres, because the buildings were treated as engineering projects.

Read:

Study links data centres to heat island effects worldwide

"Architects have a ton of value to add to the data center conversation, and I think that they got left out because it was possible to build buildings just based on efficiency," he said. "Data centres are so new that we're still figuring out what they look like."

However, he believes that now is the time to be giving more thought to how they look.

With construction already a huge source of carbon emissions, it may be that the best design when it comes to data centres is not building at all. But right now the market is saying build.

"It's not like we're not going to have data centers," said English. "The conversation today should be how to make sure that these are thoughtfully integrated into our lives."

"The architecture of the building does matter"

Until the AI bubble pops – as investors have warned – or an unlikely national referendum on the buildings happens, they look set up to keep going. So what role should architects play?

At present, architect involvement in data centre design often comes from corporate firms large enough to have a full data centre division. Gensler is one of the design-forward firms that is competing for data centre commissions.

It is currently designing a 7.5 GW hyperscale data centre in Utah for O'Leary Digital, and a cluster of five data centres for Menlo Digital in Arizona. At both sites, renders show facade treatments designed to improve the appearance of the buildings – striated facades to match the desert mountains in Utah and Corten steel in Arizona.

This move towards beautification or – in some cases, camouflage – represents one of the main ways architects are having an impact on these buildings.

"I think with good design, with proper architectural gestures, you can either make these buildings blend in or stand out, and I think that it's going to come up more and more as these buildings need to become a little bit more local," Gensler critical facilities practice leader Rob LoBuono told Dezeen.

"The architecture of the building does matter," continued LoBuono. "We really do find that a well-designed building has a strong impact in the community, even if the current opinion of them is, you know, fluid."

Otero Verzier, for her part, doesn't believe that the role of the architect should be reduced to facades.

"The idea that the most architects can do is design a facade is quite sad and says more about the lack of ambition of the profession than about the reality of data centres," said Otero Verzier.

"If, as a profession," she added, "we want to be completely irrelevant, then we can focus on designing facades for data centres."

Integrating data centres into urban schemes

During the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, architecture studio Grimshaw presented an integrated urban plan based around data centre development, bringing the typology firmly into conversations around speculative architecture.

Informed by a real project with developer Goodman, the proposal positions the data centre development as "the catalyst of a mixed-use renewal precinct – next to homes, studios, shops and even an urban farm". The proposal would pump the data centre's waste heat back into the surrounding buildings.

"Close quarters aren't a liability; they're the key that lets resources circulate instead of being wasted," said Grimshaw in the brief.

Legacy Investing's English told Dezeen that it was already developing several data centres integrated into wider mixed-use schemes, while the architecture studios we spoke to were broadly positive about the concept.

Unsurprisingly, the biggest data centre developers don't seem to be paying much attention to the thinking coming out of architecture biennales.

Efficiencies and monumental boxes are, and will probably remain, the norm.

Corgan data centre studio leader Tom Kruger said that integrating data centres within other structures and wider developments is an "exception and not the rule". He explained that concerns over security and power mean that remote locations are preferred.

"A big part of that is aiming for security and sound isolation," he told Dezeen.

Read:

Gensler designs Corten data centre to have "meaningful civic contribution"

A more realistic vision for mixed-use data centres probably looks closer to a contemporary tech campus than the Grimshaw model. Most of the architects Dezeen spoke with mentioned landscaping or parklands around the data centres, though they noted these plans run up against security concerns.

Both largely sterile and industrial in size, data centres represent a unique sort of infrastructure.

Rather than likening these buildings to warehouses or power plants, English compared data centres to parking infrastructure. He believes that they can be integrated into buildings or placed underground, and not just housed in standalone buildings.

"Parking to me is an interesting analogy because parking can be an entire building; it can be part of a building," said English. "In that way, compute can be part of a building; it can be a whole building."

Of course, parking lots have more often than not been blights on the urban and suburban landscape.

Elevated data centres

Recent projects, such as an SOM data centre skyscraper in Kansas City, show that some developers are pushing beyond the typical horizontal spread, especially where, like in this case, rural zoning laws have made developing sprawling hyperscale centres difficult.

However, architects Dezeen spoke to said building tall makes little sense, with the high price tags and sensitivity of the servers, the need for easy maintenance and the speed of building.

Most large data centres are built in areas outside of cities, with plenty of land – and land usage is a large part of the public's complaint.

Kruger, who has worked in the field for 16 years, said that he does see these centres becoming more "elevated" from an architectural perspective, though mainly through technologies that make them more energy efficient.

Other companies have proposed using older structures, as with Terawulf's plans to build a data centre in a decommissioned Kentucky smelter.

Microsoft has built data centres using mass timber in a show of healthier building materials. Meanwhile, their energy demands have revived talks of nuclear energy integration in the United States.

"Repositories of collective knowledge"

Otero Verzier envisions a more distributed future in which data centres are not commercial concentrations but public "repositories" of knowledge.

"As long as data centres start being designed with attention to the diverse ecologies of data – cold, hot, long-lasting, and temporary, open, public or private – to the limits and rhythms of the planet and its inhabitants, we can begin to develop more relevant architectures that do not necessarily look like closed-off boxes or bunkers, but instead take the form of public institutions.

If architecture can help reimagine the way these buildings look and function, through the largesse of developers concerned about buildings – or just concerned about their reception – perhaps the way they're used can change too.

Dezeen Showroom: local production, repairability and honest design are foregrounded in Norwegian brand Hegren's Knekt floor lamp.

Designed for the contemporary home, where people might use an armchair to work in as much as relax in, the Knekt lamp provides directional light that is easily angled and height-adjusted.

Like all of Hegren's products, it is designed with a focus on repairability and longevity, using standard components as much as possible so they can be replaced if needed.

Its form is intended to be pure and easy to understand, with a lampshade bent from a single laser-cut sheet of locally sourced aluminium and an aluminium arm and body.

"As a designer, I work within clear constraints – letting material, production and function shape the design from the beginning," said Hegren founder Henrik Grevstad.

"With Knekt, the open construction is both a functional consideration and an important part of the design. The structure is kept visible rather than hidden, giving the lamp a clear and honest character while remaining visually light."

Among Knekt's other practical features are an E27 socket for straightforward bulb replacement, an off-switch integrated into the lamp head for easy access, and flat-packed shipping with no-tool assembly.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Stanton Williams has completed two boarding houses for girls at Winchester College, wrapping courtyards with gabled brick buildings that reference the historic layout and architecture of the 640-year-old site.

Winchester College was originally founded in 1382, and the project is its first new boarding complex since 1912. It is also the first in its history designed for girls since the school moved to co-education in 2022.

Stanton Williams aimed to ground the scheme in both the site's historic architecture and the "culture of the college", using familiar materials and a layout based on its historic buildings and cloisters.

"We started by trying to understand Winchester on its own terms – not just its buildings, but how the college works and how pupils learn and live together," the studio's principal director Kaori Ohsugi told Dezeen.

"Because these houses are for sixth formers, we were also interested in the space between a school and a college – somewhere that provides comfort and security, but also encourages independence, conversation and the exchange of ideas," she added.

"That thinking shaped the courtyards, cloister and sequence of shared spaces, so the architecture supports the culture of the college rather than simply providing accommodation."

The two boarding houses form an S-shape that encloses two courtyard gardens on either side, with rows of gable roofs helping break down the massing of the blocks.

Overlooking the central courtyards are two back-to-back dining halls with fully glazed walls and skylit timber ceilings, which can be united as a single large space via a movable partition wall.

"Each house has its own dining hall – its own heart, in a sense – but the wall can open and the two courts, the two communities, come together," Ohsugi explained.

"It's a small architectural move, but it carries the whole idea of the project, two houses that are distinct but never separate," she added.

Read:

David Kohn Architects curves University of Oxford college building around three-sided quadrangles

Alongside the dining areas, the ground floor of the blocks accommodates communal and staff spaces, while above, two floors of bedrooms are organised off central corridors to either overlook the courtyard or the surrounding campus.

Brickwork on the exterior of the blocks references the college's Victorian boarding houses, with varying bonds, textured areas and patches of flint incorporated into the garden walls.

Inside, this is complemented by warm oak panelling incorporating perforated acoustic panels. This matches the glue-laminated timber beams of the dining halls.

"Brick was never in question – it's what the Victorian boarding houses are built from, supplied here by brick manufacturer York Handmade as a blend of four colours," explained Ohsugi.

"We varied the bonds according to how each part of the building is used," added Ohsugi. "Flemish bond at ground level, where people experience the wall at close range, references Antrim House and the historic core."

"A vertical stretcher bond marks the transition at the cloister openings, and 'hit-and-miss' brickwork sits in front of the staircase windows, giving soft, dappled light and a degree of privacy without feeling closed off," she added.

Stanton Williams is a Stirling Prize-winning London architecture studio founded by Alan Stanton and Paul Williams in 1985.

Its previous projects include a retirement complex overlooking Hampstead Heath in London and the renovation and extension of the Grade II*-listed Rhodes House at the University of Oxford.

The studio won the Stirling Prize in 2012 for the Sainsbury Laboratory in the botanic gardens of Cambridge University.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Populous has unveiled its design for the Rach Chiec Stadium in Ho Chi Minh City, which will become the country's national stadium.

Set to be built on the outskirts of the city, the stadium will be the largest in the country when completed, with around 30,000 seats more than the current record holder – the Mỹ Đình National Stadium.

The stadium will be wrapped in a diamond-patterned facade that, according to the studio, was informed by the shape of Nipa Palms that grow alongside rivers in the area.

It will be covered by a fully retractable roof that will allow the playing area to be environmentally controlled, while also shielding the surrounding residential areas from noise.

Rach Chiec Stadium is designed to host team sports such as football, but also "90 per cent of Olympic sports". It forms part of a wider plan to improve the country's sporting facilities with the aim of hosting major events including the Southeast Asian Games, Asian Cup and potentially a future Olympics.

The stadium will be built as part of a 200-hectare Rach Chiec National Sports Complex, masterplanned by Populous, which will also include an 18,000-seat arena.

Read:

Populous completes Buffalo Bills stadium in New York

"The stadium and arena design are informed by the masterplan for the entire precinct, providing anchors for a park-like experience, supported by commercial offerings and activations," said Populous senior principal Andrew Tulen.

"We are focusing on making the venues accessible, well connected and flexible to provide a variety of experiences for all demographics."

One of the world's most prolific stadium designers, Populous is currently designing stadiums for the Tampa Bay Rays professional baseball team in the USA and a stand for Wrexham AFC in the UK.

It is also currently renovating the "home of Indian cricket" in Kolkata, Estádio da Luz stadium in Lisbon for Benfica and the King Fahd Sports City Stadium in Riyadh.

item.content:encoded:
One of the oldest surviving pharmacies in the world, Florence's Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella, has appointed Italian design duo Formafantasma as creative directors.

Their new role will see studio founders Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin focus primarily on the company's products.

The studio aims to unravel their hidden histories and inform new launches, while also sharing input across Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella's packaging, communication, retail spaces and events.

"Our intention is not to redefine Santa Maria Novella through a new image, but to build from what already exists, understanding what has allowed it to remain relevant since 1221 and how this can inform its present and future," Formafantasma said.

"This means examining how its history is communicated, how new products are developed, and how the different expressions of the company can form a coherent whole."

The Officina was founded in 1221 by Dominican friars, who grew medicinal herbs and used them to prepare remedies, balms and ointments for the infirmary of Florence's Santa Maria inter Vineas church.

Over the centuries, it became a public pharmacy, official supplier to the Medici court and later a purveyor of cosmetics and fine fragrances, making it one of the oldest continuously operating pharmacies in the world. Today, it functions largely as a perfumery.

"The Officina is not simply defined by its longevity, but by the accumulation and transmission of knowledge across generations, embedded in ingredients, formulations, techniques, objects and spaces," Formafantasma said.

"Working with such an accumulation raises questions close to our own practice, particularly how it is preserved and transformed, how materials carry their own histories, and how an institution can advance without treating its past as static."

Read:

Formafantasma announced as ecology advisor to Serpentine Galleries

Material legacies are a well-trodden path for the design duo, known for its research-heavy deep dives into specific materials, whether charting the global impact of the forestry industry or unpacking wool production and our surprisingly symbiotic relationship with sheep.

For the Officina, the aim is for Formafantasma to apply this same forensic approach to materials and sustainability to the company's own uninterrupted production heritage in order to inform its future.

"Their role will be that of curators, attentive to the knowledge the Officina has safeguarded for eight centuries, made of ingredients, formulas and craft, and to the ways in which it can continue to evolve," the company said.

This isn't the first time that an institution has brought Formafantasma on board as an advisor in recent months. In July, the duo was also announced as the first-ever ecology advisor to London's Serpentine Galleries, where the designers previously hosted their Cambio exhibition.

item.content:encoded:
A former tile warehouse in Accra, Ghana, has been transformed into the headquarters of the African Futures Institute, an independent architecture school founded by Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko.

Designed by Lokko with designer Fred Swart and architects Patrick Gentilezza, Patti Anahory and Laurence Lord, the renovated building contains research and education spaces for the school and cultural spaces for the public to gather.

Situated in the neighbourhood of Osu, it is the first time the African Futures Institute has had a permanent home, after operating through partnerships and temporary spaces since its establishment in 2021.

"The refurbishment gives an existing commercial building in Osu a new civic life as a permanent centre for education, culture and public programming," African Futures Institute told Dezeen.

"Through lectures, exhibitions, workshops, screenings and gatherings, it creates a place where African Futures Institute's work can connect directly with the everyday life and rhythms of Accra," the institute continued.

"We hope people experience it as a framework for cultural activity rather than a conventional institutional building. Above all, it is intended to encourage learning, encounter and the exchange of ideas."

Read:

Lesley Lokko launches Nomadic African Studio as "a space to think about architecture differently"

Believed to have been constructed in the late 1950s or early 1960s, based on local oral history, the building envelope of the former tile warehouse was preserved and restored.

Skylights were added to the roof and new wall openings were designed to rationalise the facades.

Interior spaces were organised around the Urban Room, a multi-purpose flexible space that can operate as a lecture hall, studio, cinema, workshop and exhibition hall.

Rammed earth was used in the flooring and for a wall that extends the length of the building, which was finished with linseed oil.

Locally sourced clay bricks, quarry dust, hardwood, metalwork and precast concrete were used elsewhere in the building to form a material palette that complements the industrial former warehouse.

Last year, Lokko and the African Futures Institute launched the Nomadic African Studio educational program, which will continue operations in the new headquarters.

Lokko became the first African woman to win the RIBA Gold Medal in 2024 and was named on Time magazine's list of the 100 most influential people in the same year.

The photography is by Alix McIntosh.

item.content:encoded:
Anonymous London design duo City Girls creates one-off lighting out of reclaimed lace, coat hangers and scale models scavenged from eBay, Facebook Marketplace and the side of the road.

City Girls (stylised as city.girls.xp) is the studio and alias of two unnamed artists, who started making lamps together two years ago after bonding over a shared love of old knickknacks.

The north London duo are making a name for themselves by crafting one-of-a-kind pieces out of everything from discarded sequins to chains and feathers sourced second-hand on the internet or in real life, which at one point left them rooting through the debris of a smashed-up toy on the street.

Once each lamp is complete, it is affectionately named something like Pamela, Jean or Allegra, to give it a distinct identity.

Among the duo's growing collection is Zoe, a tall floor lamp characterised by a gridded metal frame wrapped in old jersey fabric, and embellished with goose feathers extracted from a hat.

Sabine, the pair's first working lamp, features a base crafted out of a fragment of an old chrome chair, topped with a translucent shade made of a fibreglass model boat.

Lola and Nina are a pair of boxy lamps cloaked with Glomesh sequins, a material that was also draped over the metallic Raquel.

City Girls has previously described the process of cobbling together its lighting as akin to the act of getting dressed, throwing together a mismatched outfit.

This visual style is especially clear in curving Virginia, made from old metal chair legs and crowned with a swan-like arched green head.

The duo also has a penchant for objects that show signs of fabrication through welds and seams, or anything else that nods to their former purpose.

City Girls named themselves after a Victorian novel by radical author Margaret Harkness called A City Girl, which details vivid descriptions of 1880s London streets.

Read:

Billy Easter's Gel Lamp shifts colour using transposable slides

The studio has been steadily growing its presence in the UK capital.

Over the summer, local interior designer Jermaine Gallacher curated the exhibition Ten Lamps by City Girls at the Ragged School, London Bridge.

During this month's London Design Festival, a wealth of other collectible design was on display in various city-wide exhibitions.

Among them was the second-ever Studio Iron show in South Kensington, curated by artist Isamaya Ffrench and featuring pieces by designers including Andu Masebo, Barnaby Lewis and Jane Wright.

The photography is courtesy of City Girls.

Dezeen Courses: for our latest roundup, we've selected five architecture-related courses recently featured on Dezeen Courses.

This roundup includes programmes that enhance various skills, from masterfully using specific materials to training architectural AI models.

These postgraduate and short courses take place at institutions such as the Royal Danish Academy, the School of the Art Institute of Chicago and Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne.

Below are five architecture courses featured on Dezeen Courses:

Master of Architecture/Interior Architecture at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago

The Master of Architecture/Interior Architecture course at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago offers students the opportunity to enhance their understanding of architectural history, theory and technique.

The course is accredited by the National Architectural Accrediting Board (NAAB).

Find out more about the course ›

Digital Timber Construction at Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL)

The Digital Timber Construction course at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL) focuses on using wood as a sustainable alternative to non-bio-based materials.

The four-day short course is suitable for architects, engineers, contractors and timber manufacturers and is hosted by the school's Laboratory for Timber Constructions.

Find out more about the course ›

Confluence Cycle 2 at Confluence Institute

The Confluence Cycle 2 course at Confluence Institute is a two-year programme that maps out a range of approaches to architecture through workshops led by guest professors.

The course is validated at RIBA Part 2 level by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) and upon completion, students have access to the institute's diploma studio.

Find out more about the course ›

Train Your Own Architectural AI-Model – Advanced level at My ArchiSchool

The Train Your Own Architectural AI-Model – Advanced level course at My ArchiSchool enables participants to develop LoRA techniques that help them train AI models.

Coding skills are not required to apply for this course, which is open to students of My ArchiSchool's Level 8 or above.

Find out more about the course ›

Architecture and Extreme Environments at the Royal Danish Academy

The Architecture and Extreme Environments at the Royal Danish Academy offers architectural training through a scientific approach, focusing on how the built environment can better the world.

The course works in collaboration with local manufacturers and focuses on site-specific design.

Find out more about the course ›

item.content:encoded:
Chinese studios HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan, China, which is connected by a 360-metre-long raised walkway.

Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that narrows to 21 metres at the ends.

The hotel is formed of numerous buildings connected by a walkway raised 4.9 metres above ground. According to the studios, this horizontal layout is a nod to the history of the site and an attempt to recreate a village-like neighbourhood.

"We fictionalised a village to continue the functional essence of 'dwelling'," HB Architects and Nature Times Art told Dezeen.

The raised guest rooms were also designed to reference local housing, which is often supported on pilotis.

However, the columns supporting the structures were deliberately hidden to highlight the visual dominance of the horizontal slab that runs through the site.

The hotel's entrance opens into a courtyard with a lake at its centre and a "water curtain" that falls from surrounding walkway.

Guests then walk up stairs to the raised walkway that passes around courtyards and gardens to get to the rooms. A large pool occupies the tip at one end of the raised platform.

"The building offers more than just one kind of experience," said the studios. "You have to walk through it yourself to really get it."

Read:

Hotel Wuxi MGallery Collection informed by historical poet's home

While the rooms are arranged in blocks surrounding the raised walkway, more functional spaces were placed below the slab.

The upper blocks were painted earthy yellow, while the lower floor and walkways were painted terracotta red as a reference to the surrounding landscape.

"We deliberately chose to avoid white buildings," said HB Architects and Nature Times Art. "The colours we use in this building show how we think about nature."

"The main colours relate to our design keywords—'earth' or 'nature'," they continued.

HB Architects and Nature Times Art are architecture and interior practices based in Shenzhen.

Elsewhere in China, WATG and Wimberly Interiors have completed a boutique hotel in Wuxi's Dangkou Ancient Town, and BLUE Architecture Studio has transformed a cluster of new and old buildings in Yangzhou into a hotel complex.

The photography is by Guowei Liu.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: the robust, precision-engineered quality of a restaurant kitchen can be recreated at home with Fisher & Paykel's latest Professional Style appliances.

The Professional Style appliances are one of three product design styles in the New Zealand brand's luxury range, alongside the Minimal and Contemporary offerings.

Fisher & Paykel aimed to bring the best qualities of professional cooking environments into the home, while offering the refinement and integration befitting a bespoke domestic kitchen.

High-grade stainless steel surfaces, easy-to-grab bull-nose handles and precise temperature and humidity controls characterise the products, which include ovens, hobs, refrigerators and wine cabinets.

Flush installation, smooth junctions and fine 2-millimetre gaps deliver on refinement, either imbuing products with an architectural presence of their own or concealing them seamlessly behind cabinetry.

"With the Professional Style, the intention is not for the appliance to disappear, but for it to feel completely resolved within the kitchen," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.

"The stainless-steel presence is deliberate, but so is the precision: the way the product aligns, the way it sits with surrounding cabinetry, and the way its proportions support the broader composition," he continued.

Fisher & Paykel identified the sights, sounds and rhythms of professional kitchens – "the movement of pans, the weight of metal in the hand, the choreography of preparation and service" – as part of their appeal and worked to translate those qualities into the design through robustness and tactility.

The design features precision-engineered dials on the cooktops and range cooker, and carefully calibrated oven doors and telescopic rails.

The Professional Style is part of Fisher & Paykel's vision to bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners,
supporting the creation of bespoke kitchens with a cohesive aesthetic while delivering the same levels of performance.

The brand explained that this shift to seeing the kitchen as a social space with connected dining and living functions means appliances now need to be considered not only as tools, but also as design elements.

"Luxury is increasingly personal," said Fisher & Paykel. "Kitchens are no longer singular expressions of status or function, but more personal reflections of architecture, material preferences and ways of living."

"Fisher & Paykel's appliance design styles — Minimal, Contemporary and Professional— are crafted to support different forms of architectural expression."

In contrast to the Professional Style appliances, the Minimal and Contemporary Styles have a quieter visual presence, making use of smokey dark or lightly reflective silver-grey glass and slim or no handles.

Professional Style products come in a universal width of 76 centimetres for easy configuration.

Fisher & Paykel was founded in New Zealand in 1934. Find out more about the brand and its Professional Style luxury appliances on its website.

item.content:encoded:
US studio Coughlin Scheel Architects has completed the cedar-clad Surf Road House, lifting it 10 feet above the ground because of environmental concerns.

The house sits on Fire Island, a narrow barrier island in New York that is accessed by ferry. Motor vehicles are largely prohibited on the island, with its delicate landscape.

Situated outside the town of Ocean Beach, the house is located within a designated Coastal Erosion Hazard Area, which is an area with shorelines that are receding a foot or more per year, according to New York's Department of Environmental Conservation.

The property originally had a 1950s house, which was razed.

Due to federal, state and local rules, the design for the new home went through an "extended approvals process".

Ultimately, the pre-existing house enabled the team to "maximize the allowable footprint and add a second storey", said Brooklyn-based Coughlin Scheel Architects.

Due to flooding concerns, the house was lifted 10 feet (three metres) above the ground by wood pilings. The pilings go deep, stretching up to 35 feet (10.6 metres) below grade.

Rectangular in plan, it has a boxy form that is broken up with elements such as overhangs and pilasters that "introduce rhythm, depth and shadow".

The team incorporated both vertical and horizontal striped elements on the exterior, lending a linear quality to the building.

Facades are clad in cedar siding with a colouring that alludes to dunes and driftwood, helping the house feel connected to the landscape.

Large windows on the southern facade provide views of the ocean, while the home is more opaque on the north side, which overlooks a path.

A staircase and a switchback-style ramp – both enclosed within wood-slat walls – provide access to the main entrance, which is found on the first level.

"Since Fire Island is car-free, everyone brings items from the ferry in wagons – and every house needs a ramp," the team said.

"Ramps and stairs become an integral part of the design exercise and remain part of the Fire Island entry ritual."

Inside the 2,200-square-foot (204-square-metre) house, the first level contains an open-plan room for cooking, dining and lounging.

The communal area flows onto a terrace overlooking the beach. An outdoor shower enables occupants to wash off sand before heading indoors.

Read:

Six respectfully renovated modernist homes on Fire Island

The first floor also contains a bedroom suite, and three additional bedrooms are found on the top level.

The levels are connected by an interior staircase and an outdoor spiral staircase.

Interior features include white cabinetry, wooden wall cladding and slatted ceilings that draw upon the exterior aesthetic. A curved ceiling in the entryway "adds movement and softness to the more geometric, linear architectural gestures".

The space under the house, which is enclosed by wooden screens, contains beach gear and bikes.

Other Fire Island projects include a mid-century house that was renovated by the founders of BoND to be a "machine for voyeurism" and a cedar-clad 1960s house that was renovated and expanded by Andrew Franz.

The photography is by Alan Tansey.
